articles.title: Khoa học giải thích tại sao bạn lại nhìn thấy... ma!
articles.text:
Theo Sciencing, cả ma, yêu tinh và ma cà rồng đều không thực sự tồn tại. Vì vậy, việc bạn nhìn thấy ma có thể chỉ là do quá sợ hãi.
Cần nhìn nhận thẳng thắn rằng không có bằng chứng khoa học nào chỉ ra rằng ma có tồn tại. Tuy nhiên, điều này không khiến mọi người ngừng tin tưởng rằng có tồn tại thế lực siêu nhiên kể trên. Trong một cuộc thăm dò của Huffington Post/YouGov năm 2013, có khoảng 45% người Mỹ tin rằng có ma trên đời. Ngoài ra, theo một khảo sát của Pew vào năm 2009, 18% số người được hỏi cho biết đã nhìn thấy ma.
Vậy tại sao lại có niềm tin của con người vào việc ma thực sự tồn tại trên đời? Các nhà khoa học cho rằng đây là vấn đề thuộc về yếu tố văn hóa, giống như kiểu có niềm tin cho rằng sự sống sau cái chết thực sự tồn tại.
Theo Sciencing, việc nhiều người cho rằng nhìn thấy ma là do tác dụng phụ của phản ứng căng thẳng tự nhiên. Khi quá sợ hãi và căng thẳng, ví dụ như việc đi bộ một mình vào ban đêm, nhiều người sẽ nghĩ rằng có bước chân phía sau mình.
Khi đó, trái tim sẽ bắt đầu đập nhanh hơn và nhận thức của bạn về môi trường xung quanh cũng nhạy bén hơn nhiều. Điều này khiến cho chỉ cần nghe được một thứ gì đó hoặc nhìn thấy thứ gì đó đang chuyển động là bạn quy ngay cho nó là ma.
Việc nhiều người cho rằng nhìn thấy ma là do tác dụng phụ của phản ứng căng thẳng tự nhiên.
Lý thuyết kể trên đã được khoa học chứng minh. Các nhà nghiên cứu tại Anh từng kiểm tra trạng thái tinh thần của những người từng cho rằng bản thân nhìn thấy ma. Họ phát hiện ra những người đó nhiều khả năng nhìn thấy ma (hoặc các sinh vật huyền bí khác) khi bị căng thẳng.
Nói cách khác, khi căng thẳng, cơ thể chúng ta quá nhạy bén với mọi thứ xung quanh và tưởng tượng bất kỳ thứ gì chuyển động cũng có thể là ma.
Niềm tin rằng thực sự nói chuyện được với người chết thậm chí còn phổ biến hơn là niềm tin rằng có ma trên đời. Khi trải qua một trải nghiệm quá đau buồn, chẳng hạn như việc mất người thân, đương nhiên bạn sẽ tuyệt vọng và tìm kiếm sự an ủi.
Một chuyên gia về nhận thức người Anh có tên Jennifer Whitson trả lời BBC cho biết: "Nếu bộ não không thể được kiểm soát một cách khách quan, chúng ta sẽ nhận thức có nhiều cấu trúc xung quanh mình hơn, ngay cả khi chúng không tồn tại".
Điều này có nghĩa niềm tin rằng thực sự nói chuyện được với người chết có thể đến từ việc nó sẽ giúp mang lại cảm giác thoải mái cho bạn hoặc mang đến niềm tin rằng họ đang thực sự dõi theo bạn. Tất nhiên, điều này có nghĩa là việc người thân hiện về trong giấc mơ cũng là một phần của việc bạn quá đau buồn và nhớ về họ.
Hầu hết mọi người tin rằng có tồn tại sự sống sau cái chết. Điều này khiến không có gì ngạc nhiên khi nhiều người tin rằng người chết cũng có thể xuất hiện hoặc liên lạc với chúng ta. Việc nhận thức được tiếp xúc với một hồn ma có thể là một phần của quá trình đau buồn bình thường và thậm chí có thể cho bạn biết về cách não bộ hoạt động trong một tình huống căng thẳng sẽ như thế nào.
Những hiện tượng ma quái có thể là kết quả của những vấn đề lớn hơn trong não của chúng ta, cụ thể là chất xám.
Bí ẩn về chứng tê liệt trong khi ngủ vẫn còn chưa được giải đáp (Ảnh: Sleepcycle).
Đối với một số người, việc nghe thấy tiếng nói hoặc trải nghiệm một vài hình ảnh kỳ lạ có thể là dấu hiệu sớm của các tình trạng bệnh lý như tâm thần phân liệt.
Đối với những người trải qua nỗi đau mất mát người thân, nỗi nhớ về hình bóng của họ có thể khiến não "triệu hồi" các linh hồn như một phương thức để đối phó với chấn thương tâm lý.
Điều đó hình thành nên những "cuộc gặp gỡ" sống động giữa người sống và linh hồn, thứ được các nhà tâm lý học gọi là "giao tiếp sau khi chết".
Nó từ lâu đã nằm trong số những loại trải nghiệm huyền bí phổ biến nhất, ảnh hưởng đến cả những người hoài nghi và những người tin tưởng.
Ngay cả với những người không mắc bệnh tâm thần, những thay đổi tạm thời trong hoạt động của não cũng có thể dẫn đến việc bạn cảm thấy như "chạm trán với hồn ma".
Các nhà khoa học từng mất hàng thập kỷ, nhưng vẫn chưa thể giải mã hiện tượng "liệt trong giấc ngủ", khi vẫn giữ được cảm giác có ý thức nhưng không thể cử động.
Một số người cho rằng nó xảy ra khi não giao thoa giữa giai đoạn nhận thức có ý thức và giai đoạn ngủ REM (giấc ngủ mắt chuyển động nhanh).
Các nền văn hóa khác nhau có cách gọi tên khác nhau cho hiện tượng kỳ lạ này. Thí dụ ở Campuchia, một số người nói rằng đó là "con ma đẩy nạn nhân xuống". Trong khi ở Nigeria, người dân địa phương lại gọi nó bằng cái tên khác: "con quỷ ngồi lên lưng bạn".

articles.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera is closing in to see what happened
articles.text:
NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera is closing in to see what happened
- Date:
- November 3, 2026
- Source:
- European Space Agency (ESA)
- Summary:
- Europe’s Hera spacecraft has captured its first clear view of two asteroids involved in NASA’s historic 2022 experiment to redirect a potentially dangerous space rock. Now approaching the pair, Hera will investigate the mysterious aftermath of the collision and uncover why the asteroid shifted far more than scientists predicted.
- Share:
The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has reached an important milestone in its mission to investigate a historic asteroid collision. For the first time, its onboard camera has captured the two asteroids Didymos and Dimorphos as separate objects rather than a single point of light.
The asteroid pair is currently about 197 million kilometers from Earth. Hera obtained the new image on the evening of October 18 using its black-and-white Asteroid Framing Camera, while the spacecraft was approximately 1,280 kilometers from its targets.
"With this image, the smaller Dimorphos asteroid becomes visible for the first time," explains Michael Kueppers. "Before this acquisition, the spacecraft was still resolving the Didymos system as a single dot. But now, even though Dimorphos is made up of only around one pixel in this initial image, it is clearly well separated from its parent body."
Hera Closes In on Two Asteroids
The breakthrough image follows a successful series of maneuvers designed to slow Hera as it approaches the asteroid system. Earlier in October, the spacecraft fired its thrusters twice, with one week between the maneuvers. These adjustments reduced its speed relative to the asteroids to just 20 meters per second, allowing mission controllers to carefully manage the remaining approach.
Although the two asteroids appear tiny in the initial image, they are substantial objects. Dimorphos measures about 151 meters across, making it roughly comparable in size to the Great Pyramid of Giza. Its larger companion, Didymos, is approximately 780 meters in diameter, slightly smaller than the height of Dubai's Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest building.
Dimorphos travels around Didymos at an average separation of just 1.15 kilometers, moving at a speed of approximately 18 centimeters per second.
"For the very first time we are seeing through Hera's own eyes the very double asteroid system that the mission was designed and built for," adds mission manager Ian Carnelli.
"Our views will grow much sharper as Hera comes closer. We will unveil the first detailed images of Dimorphos -- the first object in the Solar System to have had its orbit measurably shifted by human action -- on 25 November."
Uncovering the Aftermath of NASA's Historic Asteroid Collision
Hera's arrival will give scientists an opportunity to examine the results of a groundbreaking planetary defense experiment conducted four years earlier.
On September 26, 2022, NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft deliberately collided with Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 kilometers per second. The impact blasted debris as far as 10,000 kilometers into space and shortened the asteroid's orbital period around Didymos by roughly 33 minutes.
The experiment demonstrated that a spacecraft could deliberately change an asteroid's motion, an achievement with potentially enormous implications for protecting Earth from future asteroid threats.
However, the collision also produced results that scientists are still trying to fully explain. The asteroid's orbital change was substantially greater than computer simulations had predicted, raising questions about its physical properties and how it responded to the impact.
Researchers still do not know whether DART left a crater on Dimorphos or significantly altered the asteroid's overall shape. They also need more precise measurements of its composition, internal structure, and mass to understand why the collision was so effective.
Answering these questions is essential for transforming the 'kinetic impact' approach into a reliable planetary defense strategy.
Hera Prepares for a Detailed Asteroid Investigation
Over the coming months, Hera will carry out a detailed 'crash site investigation' to uncover what NASA's collision actually did to Dimorphos.
The spacecraft will use a collection of scientific instruments to examine the asteroid and its surroundings. It will also release two small satellites, known as 'CubeSats', each approximately the size of a shoebox, to gather additional observations from much closer distances. The investigation is expected to eventually include landing operations.
Together, these measurements should help scientists better understand how asteroids respond to high-speed impacts and improve predictions of how future deflection attempts might work.
Meet the Hera Space Companion
Anyone interested in following Hera's journey can explore the mission through the Hera Space Companion. More than a conventional AI chatbot, this interactive communication platform is connected to the mission and designed to make the European Space Agency's first planetary defense mission accessible to the public.

articles.title: 'OGame' developers explain how the browser-based sci-fi game has lasted 24 years ahead of the huge Orion update
articles.text:
'OGame' developers explain how the browser-based sci-fi game has lasted 24 years ahead of the huge Orion update
If you were on the Internet in the early 2000s looking for free browser games to play, OGame was a blooming sci-fi strategy sensation that couldn't be ignored. With online servers providing the structure for a living and evolving universe where players fought, traded, and created empires from scratch, its limited visual presentation was no issue.
Times have changed, but GameForge hasn't gone anywhere. OGame has been ported to mobile devices, and content updates have kept it alive and fresh for much longer than a plethora of installable MMO games.
With the Orion update, which will hit the newly launched universes (servers) on November 6, OGame is introducing conflicts against non-player-character (NPC) enemies, wave-based battles, co-op missions, and completely new systems that can also be disrupted by other players.
The game's endurance and such a major reinvention are stunning achievements, so we asked GameForge's Martin Liedtke (Director, Products of Browser Games) and Enrico Mareth (Senior Project Manager for OGame PC and Mobile) about the many challenges of working on OGame alongside the community for so long, what Orion is bringing to the table, and what's next for this worldwide phenomenon.
Some quotes have been editorialized and lightly trimmed for better flow.
"OGame has an enduring core: You build an interstellar empire, and your decisions matter... Keeping it fresh means adding meaningful choices to that foundation," said Liedtke. "Orion adds missions against automated opponents (PvE) alongside missions open to other players (PvP)... It supports different appetites for risk."
The GameForge veteran noted, however, that it's the community that "supplies another kind of freshness" after the studio releases the new content. "We develop the systems; players create much of the history."
Part of this approach is keeping tabs on how very different kinds of players approach what's available. "Some commanders concentrate on their economy; others enjoy expeditions or carefully coordinated fleet operations... Orion follows that approach; more experienced players can dig into fleet composition, progression, and cooperation. The aim is to offer worthwhile choices."
Liedtke also noted that "OGame's PvP has become a sophisticated contest of information and coordination" over time. Some players like to scout targets and organize combined attacks when enemy fleets are vulnerable. Those battles resolve automatically, but it's the planning that "can be remarkably intricate," especially after so many years of updates.
The PvE in Orion doesn't sacrifice any of those intricacies or density. In fact, it's adding a "more structured layer" that gives players clear objectives. In most cases, they'll have to cooperate to obtain better rewards. "There is a strong case for introducing that kind of cooperative PvE earlier. It gives players another reason to build and use fleets together."
Over two decades later, how people choose to engage with OGame has changed, pushing GameForge to consider supporting new platforms. Today, mobile devices have become essential to free-to-play games' success over time.
Mareth told us their importance "has made touch controls, navigation, and clarity on smaller screens central development considerations," even if thousands of players still remain attached to PC as their main platform. "We're currently working on a design overhaul of the app, combining what we've learned with players' feedback."
Liedtke also said there is more overlap between PC and mobile players than you might imagine.
"The same player might check their empire on a phone and spend a longer session planning in the browser." Liedtke also noted that "Different playstyles also have different needs," adding that activities like mining and trading fit "comfortably" into short mobile sessions, but complex fleet operations benefit from sitting in front of one's PC.
While it's a game of interstellar conflict and sci-fi spaceships, OGame does take a lot of inspiration from real-life science, even if it stretches that science well past its limits. "When ships are destroyed in battle, the debris field can form a moon around a player's planet," explains Liedtke. "The chance (of that happening) is linked to the real lunar cycle: it is higher around a full moon than a new moon."
He noted it's a "playful connection" to astronomy, "rather than a simulation of how real moons form," but the developers thought it was cool to influence the game via things that happen in our own sky.
This possible in-game "event" also led to one of the best examples of player ingenuity in OGame: Moonshots. Liedtke explained that "players organize deliberate battles and exchange sacrificial fleets to help one another obtain those valuable moons. They have turned destruction into a cooperative project. For a designer, the lesson is to examine what players can achieve together, as well as what an individual action rewards."
As the team figured out how to develop "the more imaginative side of science fiction" in OGame's universe, they also decided to explicitly use deuterium for fusion research and as fuel. Star Trek fans will recognize this as the starship fuel of that universe, but it is a real substance: one of two stable isotopes of hydrogen. "Those scientific references give the universe familiar foundations," remarks Liedtke.
In OGame's shared galaxy, Orion is introducing "anomalies" as a central new feature, which Liedtke described as "mission sites you uncover with a new scanner" before it's required to send in ships. "Combat missions ask you to hold position against waves of automated fleets; peaceful missions put your cargo ships to work collecting rewards." The twist is these missions are open to co-op... but also to rival commanders that can attack the objectives marked as PvP. While you can theoretically ignore them, better rewards await for daring commanders.
With PvE bringing all sorts of new design opportunities to the table, Liedtke pointed out the Orion update "gives us a foundation to learn which kinds of missions players find rewarding" as GameForge looks to the strategy MMO's future. "Personally, I would like to explore encounters that make commanders reconsider what to send and how to work together. Discovery becomes more interesting when it changes your plan."
Sounds exciting, though Liedtke quickly added that this isn't an official announcement of future features.
OGame's 25th anniversary is in 2027, and while the team is tight-lipped on what the team has planned, Liedtke noted that "Reaching a quarter of a century in 2027 will be an extraordinary moment for OGame. We owe that longevity to the team's continued work and, above all, to the players who keep building empires, forming alliances, and giving this universe its stories."
OGame is available on PC (via browser and GameForge's own platform) and on mobile devices via the App Store and Google Play. The Orion update arrives on November 6, 2026.
Fran Ruiz is our resident Star Wars guy. His hunger for movies and TV series is only matched by his love for video games. He got a BA of English Studies, focusing on English Literature, from the University of Malaga, in Spain, as well as a Master's Degree in English Studies, Multilingual and Intercultural Communication. On top of writing features and other longform articles for Space.com since 2021, he is a frequent collaborator of VG247 and other gaming sites. He also serves as associate editor over at Star Wars News Net and its sister site, Movie News Net.

articles.title: Sấm sét là gì? Tại sao có sấm sét?
articles.text:
Một hiện tượng thiên nhiên đặc biệt phổ biến xảy ra ở khắp mọi nơi trên Trái đất của chúng ta, đó là sấm sét. Nó là một luồng điện cực mạnh và sẵn sàng phá hủy mọi thứ mà nó phóng xuống. Những trận mưa dông, những đám mây đen u ám trên bầu trời kéo theo những luồng điện cực đại phóng các tia chớp giữa các đám mây luôn chờ nơi phù hợp để tạo bệ phóng xuống mặt đất mà con người đang sinh sống. Đó chính là sấm sét.
Sét hay tia sét là hiện tượng phóng điện trong khí quyển giữa các đám mây và mặt đất hay giữa các đám mây mang các điện tích khác dấu, đôi khi còn xuất hiện trong các trận phun trào núi lửa hay bão bụi (cát). Khi phóng điện trong khí quyển tia sét có thể di chuyển với tốc độ 36.000km/h.
Sấm hay sấm sét là âm thanh gây ra bởi tia sét và là một hiện tượng thiên nhiên. Tùy thuộc vào khoảng cách và bản chất của những tia chớp, âm thanh sấm nghe được có thể dạng thanh ngắn hoặc dàng âm trầm lớn kéo dài hoặc ngắn. Tiếng sấm thường đi sau ánh sáng của tia chớp lóe lên.
Khi tia chớp lóe lên, theo sau 1 khoảng thời gian là tiếng sấm nổ, là hiện tượng mô tả rõ ràng rằng tốc độ âm thanh chậm hơn so với tốc độ ánh sáng. Vì sự khác biệt này, người ta có thể tính toán được tia chớp cách bao xa bằng đo thời gian giữa việc nhìn thấy tia chớp lóe lên và âm thanh sấm nghe được.
Sét là sự di chuyển của các ion nhưng hình ảnh của sét là do dòng plasma phát sáng tạo ra, nên có thể thấy nó trước khi nghe tiếng động vì tiếng động chỉ di chuyển với tốc độ 1.230km/h trong điều kiện bình thường của không khí còn ánh sáng đi được 299.792.458 m/s.
Sét có thể đạt tới nhiệt độ 30.000°C, gấp 20 lần nhiệt độ cần thiết để biến cát silica thành thủy tinh.
Sét là sự di chuyển của các ion nhưng hình ảnh của sét là do dòng plasma phát sáng tạo ra.
Khi hai đám mây tích điện trái dấu lại gần nhau, hiệu điện thế giữa chúng có thể lên tới hàng triệu vôn. Giữa hai đám mây có hiện tượng phóng tia lửa điện và ta trông thấy một tia chớp. Vài giây sau ta mới nghe thấy tiếng nổ, đó là sấm (do vận tốc ánh sáng nhanh hơn vận tốc của tiếng động nên ta trông thấy tia chớp trước). Khi đám mây dông tích điện đi gần mặt đất tới những khu vực trống trải, gặp một vật có độ cao như cây cối, người cầm cuốc xẻng… thì sẽ có hiện tượng phóng tia lửa điện giữa đám mây và mặt đất. Đó là hiện tượng sấm sét.
Hơn 7.000 tia sét dội xuống Hà Nội đo bằng cách nào?
Chuyên gia lý giải về hiện tượng hàng nghìn cú sét dội xuống Hà Nội trong sáng nay

articles.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 is about to reach a historic one-light-day milestone
articles.text:
NASA’s Voyager 1 is about to reach a historic one-light-day milestone
- Date:
- November 3, 2026
- Source:
- NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory
- Summary:
- NASA’s Voyager 1 is approaching an extraordinary milestone nearly 50 years after its launch, even as engineers battle dwindling power and mysterious technical problems. A clever energy-saving maneuver has extended the spacecraft’s scientific mission, while an unexplained 48-hour communications blackout recently gave NASA a scare. On November 18, Voyager 1 will reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, making even the simplest round-trip communication take 48 hours.
- Share:
Nearly 50 years after leaving Earth, NASA's Voyager 1 is approaching an extraordinary milestone that will highlight just how far humanity's most distant spacecraft has traveled. But keeping the aging explorer operational has become an increasingly difficult challenge as its power supply slowly fades.
NASA engineers recently achieved two important developments in their effort to extend the mission. In September, they completed a complex energy conservation project designed to preserve the spacecraft's remaining scientific capabilities. Then, on October 20, Voyager 1 unexpectedly resumed communication with Earth after a mysterious 48-hour interruption.
NASA Engineers Find a Clever Way to Save Power
In early September, the Voyager team successfully replaced three devices aboard Voyager 1 with alternatives that consume less electricity. The carefully coordinated operation, nicknamed the "Big Bang," took months to prepare and was completed approximately six weeks after engineers carried out an identical procedure on Voyager 2.
The upgrade is expected to extend the operating lives of Voyager 1's remaining scientific instruments, allowing the spacecraft to continue collecting valuable information from interstellar space longer than previously expected.
Both Voyager spacecraft generate electricity using radioisotope thermoelectric generators. These systems produce electrical power from the heat released as plutonium undergoes radioactive decay. As that process continues, the spacecraft gradually lose generating capacity, with each probe experiencing a decline of approximately 4 watts annually.
After almost five decades in space, that steady loss has left engineers with very little power to spare. To keep the missions operating, NASA has progressively shut down equipment that is no longer essential.
The Big Bang presented an especially difficult engineering challenge because all three replacements had to happen simultaneously. The six devices involved help maintain temperatures inside the spacecraft despite the extreme cold of space. Replacing the three original devices together was necessary to reduce electricity consumption while preserving the proper distribution of heat throughout Voyager 1.
Keeping Voyager 1's Science Mission Alive
Power limitations have already forced NASA to deactivate two of Voyager 1's scientific instruments in recent years. When the spacecraft launched in 1977, it carried 10 instruments dedicated to scientific research. Several were shut down after Voyager completed its encounters with the outer planets, while others remained active to investigate increasingly distant regions of space.
Among the areas studied was the outer heliosphere, the enormous region of particles and magnetic fields produced by the Sun. Both Voyager spacecraft have since crossed beyond this boundary into interstellar space, making them the only spacecraft ever to directly examine the environment outside the Sun's heliosphere.
Preserving their remaining instruments is particularly important because no other missions can currently collect measurements from this distant region. Without the Big Bang upgrade, NASA would have faced the possibility of shutting down another Voyager 1 instrument as early as summer 2027.
Mysterious Communication Loss Raises New Questions
Even with the successful power conservation effort, Voyager 1 continues to encounter unexpected problems.
NASA temporarily lost contact with the spacecraft on October 18 and 19, when the agency's Deep Space Network failed to receive its radio signal during two scheduled communication attempts separated by 24 hours.
The network consists of large radio antennas at three locations around the world, allowing NASA to exchange signals with spacecraft exploring the Moon and more distant destinations. At the time of the interruption, Voyager 1 was approximately 16 billion miles (24 billion kilometers) from Earth.
After two unsuccessful attempts to detect the spacecraft, its signal unexpectedly returned on October 20, roughly 48 hours after the interruption began. Communication has remained established since then, and engineers subsequently sent commands to investigate the problem.
NASA has not yet determined exactly what caused the incident. However, engineers discovered that one set of Voyager 1's thrusters had stopped operating and that the spacecraft had automatically activated its backup thrusters.
This behavior is part of a built-in safety system known as fault protection. When the onboard computers recognize a potential problem with active equipment, they can switch to backup hardware, place the spacecraft into a stable configuration, and suspend normal activities. This gives controllers on Earth an opportunity to investigate and determine the appropriate response.
"This is the first time we've seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected," said Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "We're relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened."
Voyager 1 Approaches a Historic One-Light-Day Milestone
While NASA continues investigating the communication interruption, Voyager 1 is moving toward another remarkable achievement.
Traveling through interstellar space at approximately 38,000 mph (61,155 kph), the spacecraft is expected to reach a distance of 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth on November 18. That distance equals one light-day, meaning it takes light an entire 24 hours to travel between Earth and the probe.
No other human-made object has ever reached such a distance.
The milestone also illustrates the extraordinary challenges of communicating with a spacecraft so far from home. Radio waves travel at the speed of light, so commands transmitted from Earth will require a full day to reach Voyager 1. Any response sent back will take another 24 hours, creating a total communication delay of 48 hours.
"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL.
Crossing the one-light-day threshold will not produce any physical change in Voyager 1 or its surroundings. The spacecraft will continue traveling through the same interstellar environment, unaware that it has passed a milestone of special significance to people on Earth.
Instead, the achievement serves as a powerful reminder of the enormous distances separating objects in the universe and the remarkable endurance of a spacecraft launched nearly half a century ago. Despite fading power, aging equipment, and unexpected technical problems, Voyager 1 continues its historic journey farther from Earth than any other human-made object.
Story Source:

articles.title: Dimorphos in sight: Europe's Hera probe gets its 1st look at battered space rock (photo)
articles.text:
Dimorphos in sight: Europe's Hera probe gets its 1st look at battered space rock (photo)
"With this image, the smaller Dimorphos asteroid becomes visible for the first time."
Europe's Hera planetary defense spacecraft is closing in on the binary asteroid system targeted by NASA's DART deflection test, and can now tell the two rocky bodies apart.
Hera is nearing the end of its voyage to the Didymos asteroid system, having launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket in October 2024. The spacecraft snapped the image of Didymos and the smaller Dimorphos on Oct. 18 from a distance of 795 miles (1280 kilometers) from the pair, which are currently about 122 million miles (197 million km) from Earth.
"With this image, the smaller Dimorphos asteroid becomes visible for the first time," Michael Kueppers, Hera project scientist at the European Space Agency (ESA), said in a statement. "Before this acquisition, the spacecraft was still resolving the Didymos system as a single dot. But now, even though Dimorphos is made up of only around one pixel in this initial image, it is clearly well separated from its parent body."
The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) smashed into Dimorphos in September 2022, changing the asteroid's orbit in a pioneering planetary defense demonstration. Hera's job is to survey the damage and refine our understanding of the impact, as well as the asteroids themselves.
Hera performed braking maneuvers earlier in October to slow its approach and put it on course to rendezvous with the binary system. The spacecraft is designed to make follow-up observations of the asteroids using 12 payloads, providing new insights that will prove valuable for planetary defense efforts. The mission also carries a pair of cubesats for a closer look and eventual landing on the 495-foot-wide (151 meters) Dimorphos.
For now, Hera is continuing its approach and preparing for arrival, with a big reveal expected to occur later this month.
"Our views will grow much sharper as Hera comes closer," said ESA's mission manager Ian Carnelli. "We will unveil the first detailed images of Dimorphos — the first object in the solar system to have had its orbit measurably shifted by human action — on 25 November."
Andrew is a freelance space journalist with a focus on reporting on China's rapidly growing space sector. He began writing for Space.com in 2019 and writes for SpaceNews, IEEE Spectrum, National Geographic, Sky & Telescope, New Scientist and others. Andrew first caught the space bug when, as a youngster, he saw Voyager images of other worlds in our solar system for the first time. Away from space, Andrew enjoys trail running in the forests of Finland. You can follow him on Twitter @AJ_FI.

articles.title: Hubble Telescope sees cosmic 'cat's tail' that could wrap around Earth and the sun 500 times
articles.text:
Hubble Telescope sees cosmic 'cat's tail' that could wrap around Earth and the sun 500 times
"It's a testament to how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units."
Using the Hubble Space Telescope, astronomers have investigated a cosmic cat's tail, finding it likely formed after two Pluto-sized bodies smashed together.
The feature, nicknamed the Cat's Tail, extends out from the debris disk known as Beta Pictoris which is located in a planetary system located 63 light-years away. This tail would put that of the average tabby to shame: It's so long that it could curl around the sun-Earth system about 500 times. That's about as long as 200 trillion house cats.
The major difference between our solar system and the planetary system that hosts the Cat's Tail is the latter's relative youth. While our solar system is around 4.6 billion years old, Beta Pictoris is a cosmic kitten no more than a few million years old. That means it is still host to collisions between planetary bodies similar to the ones that rocked the solar system during its infancy.
The team behind this research gained new insights into the Cat's Tail using 14 years of observations. This allowed them to solve the long-standing mystery of the violent conditions under which it formed.
"The Cat's Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies — think something like Pluto," team leader Arin Avsar of the University of Arizona said in a statement. "Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while."
Cosmic cat tail is also pleasingly fluffy
Comparing Beta Pictoris and our solar system, one thing rapidly becomes apparent: our cosmic neighborhood is relatively well-ordered. The planets orbit the sun with most space rocks neatly delegated into bands: the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, and the Kuiper belt out beyond the orbit of Neptune.
However, this is a stark contrast to the solar system's violent and chaotic youth. Back then, the solar system was host to an infant star surrounded by a swirling disk of gas and dust in which collisions between bodies called planetesimals — the building blocks of planets — were commonplace.
Astronomers can't look back to the solar system's infancy, so to learn more about how our cosmic backyard took shape, they study nearby young planetary systems. Systems like Beta Pictoris. That doesn't mean it has been quick to divulge its secrets, though.
"We think the Cat's Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it's made of," Avsar explained. "It consists almost entirely of what we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they're quite black."
This new study revealed that the feline feature is cat-like in more ways than just its shape. It's also pleasingly fluffy, Hubble observations suggest. That's because the grains that compose it are extremely porous.
"How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here no one really understands, and that's part of why we study this feature," Avsar said.
"It's possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that's how they became so porous," team member Kevin Wagner of the U of A said.
The scientists also discovered a hitherto undiscovered feature in the Cat's Tail — a warp that seems to be the result of an interaction between the trail of material and one of the planets in the system, Beta Pictoris b, a gas giant planet 10 times more massive than Jupiter.
"This gives us another line of evidence into how giant planets influence comets through their immense gravitational force," Avsar said. "It's a testament to how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units [one astronomical unit being the distance between Earth and the sun]."
The team's research was published last month in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

articles.title: Scientists discover new Alzheimer’s drug that repairs DNA damage and reduces brain inflammation
articles.text:
Scientists discover new Alzheimer’s drug that repairs DNA damage and reduces brain inflammation
- Date:
- November 2, 2026
- Source:
- King's College London
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that a drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries can tackle several key features of Alzheimer’s disease, including DNA damage and inflammation. Already tested for initial safety in humans, the experimental treatment could offer a faster path toward therapies that target the disease at its roots.
- Share:
Scientists at King's College London have identified a promising new strategy for fighting Alzheimer's disease that could address several of the condition's damaging effects at the same time. Their research suggests that an experimental drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries may help repair damaged DNA, reduce inflammation, and target biological changes associated with the disease.
The drug, known as KCL-286, produced encouraging results in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. Unlike treatments that focus primarily on the buildup of toxic proteins in the brain, this approach targets additional processes that can begin long before the disease reaches its advanced stages.
One particularly promising advantage is that KCL-286 has already completed Phase 1 human safety and tolerability trials as part of its earlier development. This could significantly shorten the path toward further clinical testing, although its effectiveness against Alzheimer's in humans has not yet been established.
"KCL-286 is a first-in-class, orally bioavailable small molecule that has already successfully cleared Phase 1 human safety and tolerability trials. This will dramatically cut down the traditional multi-year timeline required for new drug development," commented Professor Jonathan Corcoran, Professor of Neuroscience at the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience at King's College London.
The drug is a small molecule that can be taken by mouth, making it potentially more convenient to administer than treatments that require injections or infusions.
Why Alzheimer's Disease Is So Difficult to Treat
Alzheimer's disease involves a complicated series of changes in the brain, making it particularly challenging to develop effective treatments. Two of its best-known features are the abnormal accumulation of proteins called amyloid-beta and tau.
Amyloid-beta can collect into sticky deposits between nerve cells, while abnormal tau proteins can form tangles inside them. These changes interfere with normal brain function and are associated with the progressive loss of neurons, the specialized cells responsible for transmitting information throughout the brain.
Much of the effort to develop Alzheimer's treatments has focused on these two proteins. Although medications that remove amyloid-beta have demonstrated modest but measurable clinical benefits, they do not fully address the many biological processes involved in the disease.
Researchers are increasingly investigating other changes that may contribute to Alzheimer's, including damage to DNA and inflammation in the brain. Both can appear early in the disease process, making them potentially valuable targets for treatments designed to slow its progression.
In the new study, KCL-286 helped repair breaks in DNA and reduce inflammation in mice with Alzheimer's-like disease. These findings suggest that targeting several harmful processes simultaneously could offer a broader approach than focusing on amyloid-beta or tau alone.
"Our findings demonstrate that KCL-286 not only targets DNA damage but also reduces inflammation, two processes that occur very early in Alzheimer's disease progression. This highlights its potential as a disease-modifying therapy rather than simply addressing symptoms," said Dr. Maria Goncalves, who project-managed the drug development.
How Vitamin A Pathways Could Help Fight Alzheimer's
The drug works by activating a particular protein involved in the retinoic acid pathway, a biological system associated with how the body processes and uses vitamin A.
Vitamin A is best known for supporting healthy vision, but it also plays important roles in cellular development, gene regulation, and nervous system function. Retinoic acid, a substance derived from vitamin A, helps control the activity of genes involved in several essential biological processes.
Earlier research found that disruptions in this pathway were associated with the formation of amyloid-beta deposits in the brains of rats. These deposits resemble a major pathological feature of Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that the pathway may be relevant to the condition.
KCL-286 activates a specific protein within this system, offering researchers a way to influence biological processes connected to brain health and cellular repair.
The drug had already demonstrated an ability to promote the repair of DNA double-strand breaks in earlier research involving neuropathic pain, a type of pain caused by damage or dysfunction in the nervous system.
That discovery led scientists to investigate whether the same mechanism might also help address DNA damage associated with Alzheimer's disease.
Repairing a Dangerous Type of DNA Damage
DNA contains the genetic instructions that cells need to function properly. Although cells have natural systems for repairing damaged DNA, some forms of damage are particularly serious.
One example is a DNA double-strand break, which occurs when both strands of the DNA molecule are severed. These breaks can disrupt normal cellular activity and threaten cell survival if they are not properly repaired.
"DNA double-strand breaks are like a rope snapping completely in two, rather than just fraying at the edges. We found that KCL-286 promotes repair of these breaks, allowing us to target a key feature of Alzheimer's disease," said Professor Corcoran.
The researchers had another reason to suspect that KCL-286 might be useful against Alzheimer's. Previous work by the same team at King's College London identified molecular pathways shared by acute spinal cord injury and Alzheimer's disease.
Because the two conditions involve some overlapping biological mechanisms, the scientists believed that a drug developed to address nervous system damage after spinal cord injury might also improve certain Alzheimer's-related changes in neurons.
Their new findings support that possibility, showing that KCL-286 can influence several cellular pathways involved in the disease.
A Promising New Direction for Alzheimer's Treatment
The results highlight a potentially important shift in Alzheimer's research. Rather than concentrating on one hallmark of the disease, scientists are exploring treatments that address several interconnected causes of brain damage.
KCL-286 is particularly interesting because it targets DNA damage and inflammation, two processes that can emerge early in Alzheimer's progression. Its previous human safety testing also provides a potential advantage over entirely new drug candidates that have not yet entered clinical development.
However, the Alzheimer's findings remain preclinical. Additional studies and human clinical trials will be necessary to determine whether the drug can safely slow disease progression or improve outcomes in patients.
Natasha Hill, one of the first authors on the paper, said: "To develop an effective treatment for Alzheimer's disease, we need to tackle multiple aspects of the disease. KCL-286 was able to target multiple disease-relevant cellular pathways, some of which are initiated very early in the disease course."
Story Source:
Materials provided by King's College London. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Natasha Hill, Hassan Yousef Othman AlMuallim, Elouisa Maddock, Carl Hobbs, Earl Clarke, Maria B. Goncalves, Jonathan P. T. Corcoran. Treatment with KCL‐286, a first‐in‐class retinoic acid receptor‐β (RARβ) agonist, ameliorates neuronal DNA damage and inflammation in a mouse model of Alzheimer\'s disease. FEBS Open Bio, 2026; DOI: 10.1002/2211-5463.70284

articles.title: Chó nhà "đánh nhau" tay đôi với hai sư tử và cái kết bất ngờ
articles.text:
Bị con chó lao đến tấn công liên tục, con sư tử đực chỉ biết lùi lại phía sau mà không có bất kỳ phản kháng nào.
Khi đang lang thang trên thảo nguyên Tanzania ở Đông Phi, một con chó nhỏ đã có màn đối đầu với hai con sư tử.
Trong clip, một con chó đã chạy đến trước mặt một cặp sư tử rồi sủa lớn. Ban đầu, đôi sư tử không quan tâm tới sự hiện diện của con chó. Tuy nhiên, một lúc sau, con chó bất ngờ lao về phía chúng rồi tấn công khiến cả hai con vật đều hoang mang.
Trước hành động táo bạo của đối phương, con sư tử đực chỉ biết lùi lại phía sau mà không có bất cứ hành động phản kháng nào. Sau màn tấn công, con chó nhanh chóng bỏ chạy, trong khi hai con sư tử chỉ biết chằm chằm nhìn theo.
Con chó đã chạy đến trước mặt một cặp sư tử rồi sủa lớn.
Sư tử là thú săn mồi siêu hạng và là động vật ăn thịt đầu bảng chủ chốt nhờ quần thể con mồi dồi dào. Con mồi của loài sư tử thường bị chết do sự bóp nghẹt chứ không phải do hàm răng sắc nhọn của chúng. Thức ăn của sư tử là lợn rừng, lợn lòi, trâu, hươu nai, linh dương Gazen, linh dương châu Phi và ngựa vằn.

articles.title: Large Hadron Collider reveals evidence of Big Bang matter in surprisingly small collisions
articles.text:
Large Hadron Collider reveals evidence of Big Bang matter in surprisingly small collisions
- Date:
- November 2, 2026
- Source:
- CERN
- Summary:
- Scientists at CERN's Large Hadron Collider have uncovered compelling new evidence that even relatively small atomic collisions can recreate the extraordinary state of matter that filled the universe moments after the Big Bang. Known as quark-gluon plasma, this exotic substance forms at temperatures more than 100,000 times hotter than the center of the Sun, causing ordinary particles to break apart into their fundamental building blocks.
- Share:
The findings come one year after the first-ever oxygen collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). All four of the collider's major research collaborations, ALICE, ATLAS, CMS and LHCb, have now reported signs that this primordial form of matter can emerge when oxygen and neon nuclei collide.
The results challenge a long-standing assumption about the enormous forces needed to create such an extreme substance. They also offer scientists a new way to investigate the conditions that prevailed during the universe's earliest moments.
Recreating the Extreme Matter of the Early Universe
Quark–gluon plasma (QGP) is an unusual state of matter that appears under tremendous pressure and heat. At temperatures exceeding 100,000 times those at the Sun's center, particles such as protons and neutrons can no longer maintain their normal structure. Instead, they break apart into quarks and the gluons that ordinarily bind them together.
Physicists believe that this was the state of matter throughout the universe during the first millionths of a second after the Big Bang. Nearly 14 billion years later, researchers can briefly recreate these extraordinary conditions by smashing atomic nuclei together at extremely high energies inside the LHC.
For decades, scientists believed that generating this plasma required collisions involving very heavy atomic nuclei, particularly lead. Lead nuclei are more than 200 times heavier than the protons typically used in LHC experiments, making them capable of producing the intense conditions thought necessary for QGP to form.
However, recent discoveries have increasingly called that assumption into question.
Earlier this year, the ALICE collaboration, which specializes in studying quark–gluon plasma, identified another indication of QGP formation in proton–proton and proton–lead collisions. The previous year, LHC researchers had also reported the first hints of this plasma emerging from oxygen–oxygen collisions.
Now, more detailed investigations have revealed multiple signs that QGP can form in collisions involving both oxygen and neon nuclei, providing stronger evidence that the conditions required to create this primordial matter are not limited to heavy atomic collisions.
Scientists Detect Evidence of Energy Loss in Extreme Collisions
One of the clearest ways to identify quark–gluon plasma is to examine what happens when energetic quarks and gluons travel through it.
As these particles move through the extremely hot and dense material, they lose some of their energy. Scientists call this process parton energy loss, and it provides an important clue that QGP has formed.
The ATLAS collaboration clearly detected this effect by studying pairs of particle jets generated during oxygen–oxygen and neon–neon collisions. These jets are concentrated streams of particles produced when energetic quarks and gluons emerge from a collision.
Researchers observed differences in energy between the paired jets, indicating that some of the particles had lost energy while traveling through the surrounding material.
The effect was especially pronounced during more direct, head-on (central) collisions. Such impacts are expected to create a larger volume of plasma, giving particles more material to travel through and causing greater energy loss.
Preliminary ATLAS results provide additional support for this interpretation. By examining charged particles that recoil in the opposite direction from photons, researchers found a similar relationship between energy loss and how centrally the nuclei collided.
Multiple CERN Experiments Confirm the Pattern
The ALICE, CMS, and LHCb collaborations searched for the same underlying process using a different approach. Rather than focusing primarily on the energy of particle jets, they examined how the plasma appears to reduce the production of certain energetic particles.
CMS found that charged-particle production was suppressed in both oxygen–oxygen and neon–neon collisions compared with proton–proton collisions. This reduction is consistent with particles losing energy inside quark–gluon plasma and provides further evidence that the exotic material can form in collisions involving lighter nuclei.
LHCb reported another important clue in a separate study. The collaboration investigated particles containing a charm quark and a lighter quark, comparing how strongly their production was suppressed in oxygen and neon collisions.
The suppression was more pronounced in the heavier neon collisions. That is precisely the kind of behavior scientists would expect if larger collisions produce greater volumes of plasma, causing particles to lose more energy as they pass through it.
However, reduced particle production does not necessarily prove that energy loss is responsible. Other physical processes could potentially produce similar effects.
To investigate this possibility, ALICE compared the production of neutral pions, another type of subatomic particle, in oxygen–oxygen and proton–oxygen collisions.
The comparison provided unambiguous evidence of parton energy loss in oxygen–oxygen collisions, strengthening the case that even relatively small nuclear collisions can generate conditions associated with quark–gluon plasma.
More Clues Emerge From Exotic Subatomic Particles
Researchers also looked for another distinctive signature of QGP involving particles made from a heavy quark and its corresponding antiquark.
These pairs can briefly bind together following high-energy collisions. Some are more tightly bound than others, making them differently susceptible to disruption by the surrounding plasma.
By examining which bound states are suppressed and by how much, physicists can gather additional evidence about whether QGP is present.
The CMS collaboration found evidence of this varying suppression in particles called upsilon mesons, which consist of a bottom quark paired with its antiquark. The researchers identified the effect by comparing oxygen–oxygen and neon–neon collisions.
LHCb also reported preliminary evidence of similar behavior, this time using data from proton–oxygen and oxygen–oxygen collisions.
Together, these observations add another piece to the growing body of evidence that primordial plasma can emerge in nuclear collisions much smaller than those traditionally used to study it.
Unexpected Particle Patterns Offer Another Hint
The ALICE collaboration has identified yet another possible signature of quark–gluon plasma, this time involving the directions in which particles travel after a collision.
In preliminary findings, researchers observed that particles containing three quarks (baryons) showed a stronger preference for certain directions than particles composed of two quarks (mesons) during oxygen–oxygen collisions.
This behavior is known as anisotropic flow. Rather than spreading evenly in every direction, particles emerge in patterns influenced by the conditions inside the material created during the collision.
The leading explanation involves the formation of QGP. When particles with intermediate momenta emerge from this plasma, they can inherit collective motion from the quarks that make them up.
Because baryons contain three quarks while mesons contain only two, baryons can inherit more of this flow, producing the difference observed in the experiment.
This distinctive pattern provides another potential indication that the extreme matter of the early universe is being recreated in oxygen collisions.
A New Window Into the Universe's First Moments
Scientists are continuing to analyze data from collisions involving lighter atomic nuclei, searching for additional evidence of how quark–gluon plasma forms and behaves.
The findings are reshaping the understanding of the conditions needed to produce one of the most extreme states of matter known to physics. What once appeared to require collisions between massive nuclei can now be investigated through much smaller systems, giving researchers new opportunities to explore the behavior of matter under extraordinary conditions.
Meanwhile, CERN is upgrading the Large Hadron Collider into the more powerful High-Luminosity LHC. The enhanced accelerator will allow scientists to collect substantially more collision data and investigate the properties of quark–gluon plasma in greater detail.
With each new discovery, researchers are gaining a clearer picture of the remarkable state of matter that dominated the universe during its first fleeting moments after the Big Bang.

articles.title: The Star Wars Eclipse — Want to see the 2027 total solar eclipse on Tatooine? Head to Tunisia
articles.text:
The Star Wars Eclipse — Want to see the 2027 total solar eclipse on Tatooine? Head to Tunisia
From Mos Eisley to Mos Espa and the Jundland Wastes, here's where to experience the Aug. 2, 2027 total solar eclipse from Tunisia's Star Wars filming locations.
On Aug. 2, 2027, darkness will fall on Tatooine. The path of the "eclipse of the century" crosses southern Tunisia, putting several of the most famous Star Wars filming locations in the moon's shadow for up to four minutes. Around Tozeur, eclipse chasers can experience totality among the dunes of Mos Espa and the rocky Jundland Wastes, while on Djerba, locations used for Mos Eisley and Obi-Wan Kenobi's home will also briefly go dark.
Other iconic sites are tantalizingly close to — but beyond — the southern edge of the path of totality. For example, Hotel Sidi Idriss, used as Lars Homestead in the original movie and in Attack of the Clones, gets only a 99.98% partial eclipse. So too Chott el-Djerid, site of the famous "binary" sunset over the salt flats — let's hope someone gets a partial eclipse shot from this iconic site. The nearby real-life Tunisian town of Tataouine is also just outside of the path.
For Star Wars fans planning to chase the 2027 eclipse, location will be everything. Here are four filming locations firmly inside the path of totality. All times, totality durations and historical cloud cover data come from Time and Date.
1. Eriguet dunes (Mos Espa)
Location: south of Chott el-Gharsa, Tozeur Governorate, southwest Tunisia
Start of totality and duration: 10:06 a.m. CET; 2 minutes, 9 seconds
Chance of clouds: 2%
With a massive budget and three prequels to make, Lucasfilm built a new film set that would double as the Mos Espa spaceport on Tatooine for The Phantom Menace and Attack of the Clones. This is where Qui-Gon Jinn, Obi-Wan Kenobi, Jar Jar Binks and Padme get stranded, where they meet Anakin Skywalker and where the podrace takes place. Now abandoned, it's in the middle of nowhere, between two huge salt lakes and subject to the intense heat and moving Eriguet dunes — but it is firmly within the path of totality. Nearby are two other shooting locations — the Ong Jemel outcrop, where Darth Maul arrives on the scene, and Yardang, where Qui-Gon and Darth Maul battle — the first-ever lightsaber duel filmed on location.
2. Maguer Gorge (Jundland Wastes)
Location: Jebel Sidi Bouhlel canyon, Dghoumès National Park, Tozeur, southwest Tunisia
Start of totality and duration: 10:06 a.m. CET; 3 minutes, 37 seconds
Chance of clouds: 1%
Often called "Star Wars Canyon" by fans and crew, Maguer Gorge in Jebel Sidi Bouhlel doubled as the Jundland Wastes of Tatooine in Star Wars: Episode IV — A New Hope. It's where Luke Skywalker is attacked by Tusken Raiders, where Obi-Wan Kenobi first appears and where Luke and Obi-Wan discover the slaughtered Jawas. The canyon also provided the distant view of Mos Eisley — the famous "wretched hive of scum and villainy." On Aug. 2, 2027, you'll likely be pointing your macrobinoculars at the eclipsed sun rather than Tusken Raiders.
Steven Spielberg later filmed here for Raiders of the Lost Ark, including the scene in which Indiana Jones threatens to destroy the Ark with a bazooka. Just south of Dghoumès National Park is a desert oasis called Bouhlel Sdada, used for the archaeological dig scenes in Raiders.
3. Ajim (Mos Eisley)
Location: Ajim city center, Médenine Governorate, Djerba island, Tunisia
Start of totality and duration: 10:10 a.m. CET; 3 minutes, 55 seconds
Chance of clouds: 19%
Djerba Island's palm trees, beaches and Mediterranean horizons will make it a popular destination for eclipse chasers after a long totality away from the heat and crowds of Luxor in Egypt. It's also home to three notable Star Wars filming locations. The original movie's Mos Eisley footage was shot here, with Ajim doubling as a Stormtrooper checkpoint ("These are not the droids you're looking for"), the Cantina exterior, and an alley near Docking Bay 94 where stormtroopers watch the Millennium Falcon blast off. In reality, it's an abandoned bakery.
4. Amghar Mosque (Obi-Wan Kenobi's house)
Location: Ajim outskirts, Médenine Governorate, Djerba island, Tunisia
Start of totality and duration: 10:09 a.m. CET; 4 minutes
Chance of clouds: 19%
Just north of Ajim, this mosque — originally a fisherman's house — was used as a stand-in for "Old Ben's" house, where Obi-Wan Kenobi gives Luke Skywalker a lightsaber. It was used purely for photography, and no actors set foot here. It was also cut from the movie's Special Edition in 1997, so you'll only find it in the original version. Completists might also want to check out Sidi Jemour Mosque to the north, which was used for scenes with Biggs Darklighter that didn't even make the final cut. IYKYK …
How to go on a Star Wars tour in Tunisia
Tunisia's Star Wars locations are spread across the south, so the easiest way to see several is on an organized tour or with a private driver and guide. Tozeur is the main base for visiting Mos Espa, Ong Jemel and Jebel Sidi Bouhlel, with local operators offering half-day and full-day 4x4 excursions into the desert. Djerba Island is the other major hub for three sights. Longer multi-day tours typically connect Tozeur with Matmata, home to Hotel Sidi Idriss — the Lars Homestead — as well as Djerba.
One tour company, Star Wars Tours, is running a (sold-out) special departure called "Eclipse tour from the Outer Rim" that witnesses totality at the Mos Espa set. Other Star Wars-focused tour operators include Galaxy Tours, though one-day trips to the Mos Espa set from Tozeur are also available.
Where else to watch the eclipse in Tunisia
Tunisia is surely one of the most attractive destinations for the Aug. 2, 2027 total solar eclipse. Historical cloud cover is exceptionally low, while totality reaches around five and a half minutes near the centerline. It also offers established tourism infrastructure and generally lower August temperatures than Egypt, making it an obvious alternative for eclipse chasers hoping to avoid the biggest crowds around Luxor.
You can, of course, visit the Star Wars sets in the days before or after the eclipse. For Tunisia's maximum duration of totality, consider Sfax, where darkness lasts 5 minutes, 41 seconds, or nearby Chaffar Beach, with its long, open Mediterranean coastline. Offshore, the low-lying Kerkennah Islands get around 5 minutes, 39 seconds. Inland, Sidi Bouzid offers about 5 minutes, 33 seconds beneath typically dry skies, while the spectacular Roman amphitheater at El Jem gets 4 minutes, 23 seconds. On Djerba Island, meanwhile, beaches and extensive resort infrastructure make combining an eclipse chase with a conventional Mediterranean vacation particularly easy — with a view of Mos Eisley thrown in for good measure.
Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

articles.title: Loại cây kỳ lạ "lai dứa và xương rồng" trên ngọn núi cao nhất châu Phi
articles.text:
Trên ngọn núi lửa không hoạt động Kilimanjaro ở Tanzania có nhiều loài cây "độc nhất vô nhị" với hình dáng vô cùng kỳ quái.
Kilimanjaro là một ngọn núi lửa không hoạt động ở Tanzania. Đây là ngọn núi cao nhất ở Châu Phi và là ngọn núi độc lập cao nhất thế giới: 5895 m so với mực nước biển. Kilimanjaro là một phần của công viên quốc gia Kilimanjaro và là một điểm leo núi rất nổi tiếng trên thế giới.
Cây Dendrosenecio kilimanjari.
Là ngọn núi cao nhất ở châu Phi, Kilimanjaro có khí hậu khá đặc biệt, vì thế nơi này có nhiều loại cây "đột biến", quý hiếm hầu như không tìm thấy ở nơi nào khác trên Trái đất.
Một trong những loài cây nổi bật nhất trong số đó có tên là Dendrosenecio kilimanjari. Loài cây kỳ lạ này giống như một cây lai giữa cây xương rồng và dứa. Tuy nhiên Dendrosenecio kilimanjari được xếp vào loài thực vật có hoa trong họ cúc.
Cây Dendrosenecio kilimanjari được HHJohnston mô tả lần đầu tiên vào năm 1884. Loài cây này cao tới 10m, nó tạo thành một thân gỗ (đường kính khoảng 40 cm) với những chiếc lá lớn hình hoa thị trên đỉnh. Những thân cây này phân nhánh sau khi ra hoa và theo thời gian phát triển tương tự như những cây nến khổng lồ. Cây trưởng thành có thể có tới 80 nhánh.
Loài cây kỳ lạ này là một thành viên của gia đình bồ công anh và các nhà khoa học cho rằng chúng tiến hóa từ một loài cây thông thường khoảng 1 triệu năm trước. Có thể chúng ban đầu là một loài cây hình thành dưới mặt đất, nhưng theo thời gian, hạt giống của chúng đã dần được đưa lên các ngọn núi cao và cuối cùng biến thành một loài mới.
Để tồn tại trên địa hình núi cao như vậy với nhiệt độ siêu lạnh giá vào ban đêm, các cây đã tiến hóa tích trữ nước trong phần thân còn lá cụp lại khi nhiệt độ giảm xuống.
Những thân cây này phân nhánh sau khi ra hoa và theo thời gian phát triển.
Bên cạnh khả năng "chống đóng băng" tự nhiên, những cây này còn sở hữu khả năng tự cách nhiệt thông qua những tán lá khô héo và chết (đó là một phần lý do tại sao chúng trông rất khác thường).
Cây Dendrosenecio kilimanjari mọc ở vùng đồng hoang ẩm ướt ở độ cao 2700 - 3350 m và chỉ được tìm thấy trên núi Kilimanjaro.
| Kilimanjaro với 3 chóp núi lửa hình nón, Kibo, Mawensi và Shira, là một núi lửa dạng tầng không hoạt động ở đông bắc Tanzania. Mặc dù không phải là núi cao nhất thế giới, nhưng Kilimanjaro lại là ngọn núi đứng một mình cao nhất thế giới và là đỉnh núi cao nhất châu Phi. Được mệnh danh là hòn đảo trên bầu trời, Kilimanjaro có sự đa dạng sinh học khổng lồ với các loài đặc hữu bao gồm các loài Dendrosenecio và hệ thực vật khác thích nghi sống trong các điều kiện núi cao. |

articles.title: Scientists just found a loophole that could let black holes split in two
articles.text:
Scientists just found a loophole that could let black holes split in two
- Date:
- November 2, 2026
- Source:
- University of Southern Denmark
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a possible loophole in the laws that normally prevent black holes from splitting apart, suggesting that extremely fast-spinning black holes might divide into two. The surprising finding raises the possibility of an entirely new black hole phenomenon that future telescopes could potentially detect.
- Share:
Black holes are known for merging when two of them collide, but could the reverse ever happen? Could a single black hole somehow divide into two smaller ones? A new theoretical study suggests that this extraordinary possibility may not be entirely ruled out by physics, although the conditions required would be extreme.
The research, published in Physical Review D under the title "When Black Holes Admit Pair-of-pants Topologies," examines the physical laws that keep black holes intact and whether certain circumstances could allow them to break apart.
"In our study, we investigate which physical laws normally prevent a black hole from splitting into two. We also investigate if certain circumstances may allow a split to happen," says Francesco Sannino, co-author of the study and a professor of physics at University of Naples Federico II in Italy and Quantum Field Theory Center at University of Southern Denmark.
The research team also included Giacomo Cacciapaglia, a researcher with the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) at the Laboratoire de Physique Théorique et Hautes Énergies, a joint CNRS and Sorbonne Université laboratory in Paris. Additional contributors were Manuel Del Piano and Vania Vellucci, both from the Quantum Field Theory Center at the University of Southern Denmark.
Why Black Holes Normally Cannot Split Apart
One of the biggest obstacles to a black hole splitting comes from thermodynamics, the branch of physics that governs how energy behaves and how physical systems change.
A central concept is entropy, which describes how many different microscopic arrangements a system can have while appearing unchanged from the outside. Black holes have entropy, and this property places important limits on what can happen to them.
For a black hole that is not rotating, dividing into two smaller black holes would reduce the total entropy. Such a decrease makes the process thermodynamically unfavorable, helping explain why black holes do not ordinarily break apart.
However, the researchers found that the situation could change dramatically when a black hole spins at an exceptionally high speed.
Extreme Rotation Could Allow Black Holes to Split
The team's calculations suggest that rapid rotation may create a narrow opening in the physical rules that normally prevent black holes from dividing. In principle, a sufficiently fast spinning black hole could overcome the usual thermodynamic restriction.
But there is another major obstacle. Even if a black hole could divide, the two resulting objects would need to move far enough apart to avoid immediately merging again.
"But the two resulting black holes must also be able to separate rather than immediately fall back together. When we include this requirement, the window largely closes again, except possibly for black holes rotating close to their maximum possible rate," says Francesco Sannino.
The study's unusual title refers to the shape that a black hole's boundary would trace through space and time if such a split occurred. This boundary, called the horizon, would begin as a single structure before separating into two distinct branches.
Viewed across time, the resulting shape would resemble a pair of trousers, with one upper section dividing into two "legs." This is the idea behind the term "pair-of-pants topologies."
Extra Dimensions Offer Another Possibility
The researchers also investigated more unusual scenarios involving theories in which space has additional dimensions beyond the three we experience in everyday life.
Physicists have already identified objects resembling black holes in some of these theoretical models that can become unstable and start breaking apart. These possibilities suggest that the familiar rules governing black holes may not apply in the same way under more exotic conditions.
In certain cases, splitting could even become thermodynamically favorable, especially when one of the two resulting black holes is much smaller than the other.
However, a process being allowed or favored by thermodynamics does not necessarily mean it will happen. Researchers still need to determine whether such fragmentation can physically occur and what conditions would make it possible.
Could Astronomers Detect a Black Hole Splitting?
The scientists are now working to better understand how likely these events might be. The answer may depend on aspects of gravity that go beyond Einstein's theory, making the problem especially challenging.
"We cannot yet give a single probability for a black hole to split. It depends on how gravity behaves beyond Einstein's theory, and we are working to quantify this. We expect small primordial black holes to be more prone to splitting than much larger astrophysical black holes. We may detect a split indirectly: gamma-ray telescopes such as Fermi-LAT can search for signals from tiny black-hole fragments that might form during mergers," says Francesco Sannino.
Although there is currently no confirmed observation of a black hole splitting, the possibility of detecting signals from tiny fragments offers a potential way to investigate the idea. Such evidence could provide valuable clues about the behavior of gravity under some of the most extreme conditions in the universe.
Sannino is the director of the Quantum Field Theory Center (ℏQTC), which is affiliated with the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science (IMADA) at the University of Southern Denmark. He is also affiliated with the Danish Institute for Advanced Study and the Department of Physics "Ettore Pancini" at the University of Naples Federico II. In addition, he serves as a visiting professor at Durham University.
Story Source:

- Giacomo Cacciapaglia, Manuel Del Piano, Francesco Sannino, Vania Vellucci. When black holes admit pair-of-pants topologies. Physical Review D, 2026; 114 (8) DOI: 10.1103/cx69-t466

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 3, 1957: Laika the dog launches with Sputnik 2
articles.text:
On this day in space! Nov. 3, 1957: Laika the dog launches with Sputnik 2
On Nov. 3, 1957, a Soviet space dog named Laika became the first animal to orbit Earth.
On Nov. 3, 1957, a Soviet space dog named Laika became the first animal to orbit Earth. Laika was a 3-year-old stray husky-spitz mix from the streets of Moscow, and she was recruited by the Soviet space program for her small size and calm temperament.
Unfortunately for Laika, this mission was a one-way trip. The Soviets didn't design a way to bring her back down to Earth. With only 7 days worth of oxygen and a little bit of food on board, Laika launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan with a Russian Sputnik rocket. This was the same kind of rocket used to launch the first Sputnik satellite.
Laika was alive when she reached orbit, but she died shortly afterward because the spacecraft's heat shield had broken off. Laika overheated before she had the chance to die of starvation of oxygen deprivation.
Why it mattered
Laika has remained one of space history's most beloved and tragic figures. People around the world have dogs as pets who they love as members of their own families. And even nearly 70 years after this flight, it is so heartbreaking to think of Laika on that frightening journey from which she never returned.
Laika was one of many different animals that were used in early spaceflight testing. Both the U.S. and Russia launched a number of primates on flights testing early flight technology. Sadly, like Laika, many of these brave creatures did not make it back.
Unbelievably, though, some did survive the journey. For example, the chimpanzee named Ham and nicknamed the "astrochimp" survived a 1961 test flight to space. Though, the team behind that flight was so unsure of how it would go that Ham didn't get his name until after it was found that he'd survived his return.
Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.
Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.
- Chelsea Gohd Content Manager

articles.title: Would you risk your health to visit Mars?
articles.text:
Would you risk your health to visit Mars?
A recent rat study hinted that cosmic radiation could pose health risks for future Mars explorers. Live Science asks its readers whether they'd take the journey anyway.
A crewed mission to Mars could be one of humanity's greatest achievements, but getting there may come with serious health risks. Beyond the challenges of surviving in space for months at a time, astronauts would face prolonged exposure to cosmic radiation — high-energy particles in space that can penetrate the human body and potentially damage vital organs.
- Chinese lander reveals giant 'cavity' of radiation between Earth and the moon — and it could change how lunar exploration is done
- 'Everything we know about space travel is going to change within a decade': The fusion breakthrough that could unlock a path to the stars
- Scientists finally know why astronauts struggle to poop in space — and reveal a hidden risk of long-haul spaceflight
A new study suggested that cosmic radiation could pose a particular threat to heart health. Researchers found evidence that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what human astronauts might encounter during a mission to Mars and back developed more scar tissue around the small vessels in their hearts compared with rats that weren't exposed to space radiation.
Although the findings haven't been confirmed in humans yet, they add to the growing concerns about the long-term health effects of sending astronauts on long-duration space missions.
NASA and other space agencies are working on ways to eventually send humans to Mars and beyond. Given these latest findings, would you travel to Mars? Vote in the poll below, and let us know your thoughts in the comments.
Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027. Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.
