articles.title: Here’s what it’s like to use Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch
articles.text:
It’s impossible to paint a full picture of what Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 will be right now. The watchOS 27.3 developer beta just dropped earlier this afternoon, and these features are meant to be lived with in day-to-day life. We’re definitely going to do that over the next few weeks at The Verge. That said, here are some initial impressions.
Here’s what it’s like to use Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch
The watchOS 27.3 beta adds Live Rewind and Siri Recap to the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.
What’s newly available today is Live Rewind and Siri Recap. The former lets you see a transcript of the last 15 seconds, while the latter provides high-level summaries of your conversations. (The other two Audio Intelligence features have been available for the last few weeks. I wrote about those in my Series 12 review.) And as always, this is the developer beta. These features could still change quite a bit before a final version arrives for the public.
The first thing I noticed is that these features are not turned on by default. I wasn’t expecting anything different, but it’s worth remembering that these features don’t automatically turn every Apple Watch into a surveillance device. Audio Intelligence requires the latest Apple Watch hardware, a compatible version of iOS (so in this case, the iOS 27.3 developer beta), and someone has to actively choose to enable these features. You can download the beta and double-press the crown to initiate a Live Rewind. It won’t do anything. You must opt in via your iPhone’s Watch app. Same goes for Siri Recap. Enabling Live Rewind also requires an initial microphone calibration with your phone.
Privacy-wise, Apple has publicly available support documentation about its approach to these features. I’m not weighing in on how well it executes them in this hands-on. But Apple has pretty clear messaging in the onboarding process. There are quite a few customization options for when Siri Recap is active. You can get pretty granular. For example, you can have Siri Recap on only at the office during weekdays from 1PM to 4PM if that’s when you have meetings. This is hard to convey to bystanders, and I think ethical use should come with an in-person heads-up to the people you frequently interact with. (Hello, fellow Verge writers and editors.)
Live Rewind, so far, has worked as described — with the heavy caveat that I’ve only tested it in my quiet home office with my spouse. Even so, it takes a hot second to learn the timing of a double press. My spouse noticed the audible chime signaling the feature is in use, though they didn’t notice the animation. I’ll have to see how this fares in louder environments. Siri accurately captured our attempts to get my cat to roll over, though in subsequent tests, it misheard a word or two.
I’m more hesitant to comment on Siri Recap. It’s not just because I haven’t had many organic, lengthy spoken conversations yet since downloading the beta. (Siri did not deem my brief conversation with my spouse as worthy enough for recapping.) But I won’t really get a sense for how this feature feels until I’ve tested it in a wide variety of scenarios. Will it work if I talk to myself aloud? How well does it filter out gossip? How will this change how people speak to me? That’ll be the true test of this feature and Apple’s bystander privacy claims.
My first Siri Recap was for an editorial planning meeting for a story I’m working on. It was decent at identifying different topics discussed, and I was impressed that it stripped out some sensitive information. Any outsider looking at these notes would be terribly confused. Ironically, it meant that this summary wasn’t the most useful for my job.
What I will say is that I’ve been testing the Amazon Bee Frontier for the past few weeks. In the little time I’ve spent with the watchOS 27.3 beta, the differences between Audio Intelligence and the Bee are very clear. The latter has more of what I’d call an AI-forward presence. Bee, for example, offers insights about the emotional tone of a conversation. I’ve also found that the AI can be a bit judgy about insights and takeaways. Live Rewind is just a straight transcript. Apple’s said publicly that Siri Recap is meant to be highly factual notes to jog a person’s memory. That rings true based on my first one. And, as far as I can tell, there is no commerce angle for Siri Recaps, whereas Bee has an Amazon integration that surfaces buying suggestions based on conversations.
In any case, I’ll be diving deep into these features in the days to come. Let us know in the comments what you’re most curious about.

articles.title: Yvonne Bajela is bringing $17M in fresh capital to Europe's startup scene | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Yvonne Bajela knew it was time to launch her own fund. She spent more than a decade as a VC, most recently at LocalGlobe and Impact X Capital Partners, where she made bets on now-unicorn companies like the fintech Wise, the insurance company Marshmallow, and robotaxi Mooves.
On Tuesday, she announced that her own fund, Evertrue Capital, officially closed an oversubscribed $17 million Fund I.
“After more than a decade backing founders who bet everything on their ideas, it felt like time to make a bet of my own,” she said. “I wanted the independence to act on those convictions and build something that reflected my own approach to investing.”
The firm, which has already backed seven companies, will focus on early-stage investing across the U.K. and Europe. The average check size will be around £350,000, she said, with plans to back at least 20 companies over the next three years.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, she said this AI boom helped her realize that this was the right time to launch her own fund. Not only has it changed the economics of launching a company, she said, but it has created new opportunities for early-stage investors like herself. “The ability to build has been democratized,” she said. “But the ability to build something enduring remains rare.”
As TechCrunch has previously reported, the U.K.’s startup scene is having a moment. King’s Cross, for example, is one of the world’s top AI hubs, while companies like Revolut, Synthesia, ElevenLabs, and the Bezos-backed CuspAI are redefining what it means to scale and attract success in the U.K. market. For someone like Bajela, this moment means there is an opportunity to snap up investments in the next generation of top British talent early. “I think more globally significant businesses will emerge from a wider range of starting points,” she said.
However, this is also a tough market for emerging fund managers. In the U.S., it has been described as a barbell market where capital is concentrated at the top and among firms led by those who already have solid track records. Things may be slightly rosier in the U.K., as PitchBook data through the end of September shows that emerging fund managers in this region raised $7.4 billion, already surpassing the $6.2 billion they raised in all of 2025.
Still, Bajela said fundraising was a grind. The hardest rejections weren’t necessarily the outright nos. “They were the ones that came after months of conversations and significant time invested, only for the answer to ultimately be no,” she said. “Time is one of the most valuable resources a founder has, and a prolonged process without clarity has a real cost.”
Still, she said the fund nabbed five institutional backers, including the British Business Bank and Basecamp, the fund-of-funds of the investment firm Phoenix Court, which is also home to LocalGlobe. Evertrue was part of the £400 million British Business Bank’s Investor Pathways capital initiative, which saw it distribute £90 million to 10 first-time fund managers. Bajela said Evertrue wanted to raise around $13 million but saw a lot of investor interest. She decided to turn down additional investors rather than expand the fund size.
“Fund size is a strategic decision, not a measure of success in itself,” she said. “I wanted enough capital to build meaningful positions in my highest-conviction investments without creating pressure to deploy capital simply because it was available.”
Around 80% of Evertrue’s LPs are U.K. based, with the rest scattered across Europe, Asia, and the U.S. She said her international LP base represents the relationships she’s built “over more than a decade investing across markets.” It also reflects the fund’s global ambition, she said, especially since so many British founders keep their eyes on a U.S. expansion; more than half her portfolio already operates in the U.S.
Evertrue will invest mainly across AI and fintech, she said, adding that she’s “particularly interested in people with a unique insight into a problem, an unusual ability to execute, and the ambition to build something much bigger than their initial product.”
“I also pay attention to the distance a founder has traveled, what they’ve overcome, and how that has shaped their perspective,” she continued.
She’s lived in Japan as a senior investment manager at Mitsui and started her career as an analyst at Goldman Sachs. Throughout her career, she said she’s seen how “widely distributed ambition and talent are.”
“I want Evertrue to be known for the quality of the founders I back and the businesses they go on to build.”

articles.title: Bosch gives chips their own division, eyeing €5bn in sales by 2030
articles.text:
Bosch will move its semiconductor business into a dedicated division from January 2028, as the German supplier looks to expand chip sales beyond the automotive industry.
The company is targeting annual semiconductor revenue of around €5bn by 2030, it announced today. The new unit, which will be called Semiconductors, will remain part of Bosch rather than becoming a separate company.
Its chip business currently sits within the Mobility Electronics division, which will continue to handle the production of electronic control units for vehicles.
The restructuring reflects Bosch’s ambition to find more customers for its chips outside the automotive sector.
The company plans to open its manufacturing facilities to external clients and expand its foundry business, producing semiconductors for other companies.
Its target markets include robotics, factory automation and AI data centres, alongside consumer devices such as phones and wearables. Bosch says its components already play a role in controlling humanoid robots.
“With the founding of a dedicated unit, we are opening a new chapter in our more than 60-year semiconductor history,” said Erik Rein, who heads Bosch’s chip business.
Bosch has several established positions in specialised semiconductor markets. It is a leading supplier of MEMS sensors, the miniature motion and pressure sensors used in devices such as smartphones and robots.
The company also produces silicon carbide chips and custom circuits for power systems.
Its manufacturing footprint spans around 40 chip sites worldwide. Bosch has invested approximately €3bn in its wafer plants in Dresden and Reutlingen, and is spending around $2bn to convert its Roseville, California facility to silicon carbide production.
The company also plans to expand its test centre in Penang, Malaysia, through the mid-2030s. It holds a 10% stake in ESMC, the TSMC-led semiconductor joint venture building a factory in Dresden.
The move comes as Europe’s automotive industry continues to grapple with chip supply risks.
Carmakers spent part of the autumn managing shortages during the Nexperia dispute, which exposed the industry’s dependence on a limited number of suppliers.
By offering manufacturing capacity to outside customers, Bosch could help diversify Europe’s chip supply while seeking new markets for its own technology.
Bosch deputy chairman Markus Heyn said the company’s sensors are “the key” to its products and “the technological basis” for its customers’ innovations.

articles.title: Don’t be fooled by the fake hair on these famous baldies
articles.text:
Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and actor Jason Statham have a distinctive feature in common: They’re both famously bald, and that definitely hasn’t changed in the last few days. However, there are some images of the two men circulating around X, Threads, and Bluesky in which they both have substantially more hair than their usual shaved look, which in Bezos’ case appears to be very freshly transplanted. It’s all just photo editing fakery, AI or otherwise.
Those Jeff Bezos hair transplant photos are very fake
In the era of easy AI fakery, edited paparazzi photos are a reminder that not everything is what it seems.
It’s unclear how viral these posts are, but they’re prevalent enough that a few members of the Verge team have encountered them in their social media feeds. Some people who shared them claimed (or were seemingly fooled into believing) that Bezos and Statham had undergone hair transplant surgery. Generative AI tools have made this kind of photo manipulation or outright creation more accessible and convincing, and because AI labeling solutions on social media broadly suck at flagging this fakery, it’s easy to be misled unless you’re wary of everything you see online. In a world where social media shitposters can turn engagement into a revenue stream, they’re not going to stop churning out attention-grabbing fabricated nonsense anytime soon.
We don’t know if AI tools were used to make the follicled Bezos and Statham edits — none of the images I tested flagged for Content Credentials or SynthID markers. We also can’t fully establish when they were first posted or who made them, but they are definitely fake, and it only took me a couple of minutes to confirm it.
In both cases, I ran the photos through Google’s reverse image search tool. For the Bezos debunk, I found photographs of him in a similar background environment and wearing the exact same outfit (with, yes, no hair) that included a watermarked image credit at the bottom left. Searching for the credit then led me to the original photographs in their unaltered state, which were taken in 2023. Finding the original tressless images of Statham was even easier — the reverse image search immediately surfaced watermarked versions of the originals, which were snapped by a paparazzo in 2011.
There’s other evidence too if you know what to look for. The main flag is that it’s probably impossible for Bezos and Statham to be realistic candidates for hair replacement surgery anyway; it requires you to have enough “donor” hair to sacrifice from the back and sides of your head to then replant closer to your desired hairline. You can technically take it from other places (or even other people), but doing so is incredibly rare due to undesirable results and rejection concerns. Transplant patients also typically experience some pretty dramatic facial swelling for the first week or so, which Bezos shows no signs of. Wigs, toupees, and other hair systems can also be used as nonpermanent hair restoration solutions, but as someone who used to make and install them professionally, it would be an astounding whoopsie for someone as rich and connected as Bezos to go this route and still end up looking like a Chia Pet.
This isn’t the first time photo-manipulated fakery has fooled people across social media, and with ongoing generative AI advancements, it probably won’t be the last. Previous incidents gave us the viral swagged-out pope, and recent trends have seen paparazzi photographs of celebrities like Callum Turner, Harry Styles, and Noah Schnapp being manipulated to remove their shirts. These kinds of edits are typically designed to rack up likes, reposts, and other engagement — they play into our fascination with celebrities’ lives with fabricated situations that are just outlandish enough to be believable, grab our attention, and be shared around as the latest hot gossip by those who are fooled, or who simply don’t care to verify the facts.
If you’re ever unsure if there’s fakery afoot with images of famous faces, just remember that most of the convincing edits (AI or otherwise) are based on real photos that you can hunt down to verify the original source.

articles.title: Google responds to political backlash over removing search from schools that ban AI
articles.text:
Google is playing defense on Tuesday after a political backlash to its new policy surrounding use of artificial intelligence in schools.
In a blog post titled "Designing responsible AI for learning," Google said it's bringing AI into its Classroom offering with a product called Guided Learning. The New York Times published a story saying that the company will turn off search for schools that reject AI entirely.
Following the Times' story, prominent left-leaning politicians, including Sen. Bernie Sanders from Vermont and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani voiced their outrage on social media.
"Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," Mamdani wrote on X. Sanders wrote that "Google is threatening schools," referring to the policy as "extortion."
Google responded later in the day. In a post on X, the company said its new policy was meant to give schools more choice over how students interact with AI. Google said its Gemini chatbot, Gemini Notebook and search are turned off by default, and that "schools are in control," with the ability to turn them as they see fit.
"We are also updating Search for schools to make it better for learning," Google wrote. "Specifically, AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don't get quick answers to schoolwork."
The company's post didn't explicitly respond to the claim that access to search requires use of AI. However, Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the Times that "Search and AI are deeply integrated."
A Google spokesperson referred CNBC to the X post when asked for comment.
Google's broader practices have come under fire in recent years, with the company losing antitrust cases over its search and advertising businesses. Former Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan aggressively pursued Google and other tech giants, including Meta and Amazon.
Khan said in a post on X on Tuesday that Google's new AI for learning policy highlights "the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service."
It's the latest controversy related to the impact of technology on children and the role leading internet companies are playing in delivering information.
In August, Meta reached a landmark $16.7 billion settlement in its child safety trial after a number of state attorneys general accused the company of misrepresenting the extent of child mental health harms caused by apps like Facebook and Instagram.
The same month, OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens after state attorneys general launched an investigation into the company's safety practices, with Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, a Republican, filing a lawsuit in June.
The nonprofit Common Sense Media recently gave Google's AI overviews an "unacceptable risk" rating. Last month, Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Josh Hawley, R-Mo., launched an inquiry over Google's push of AI into classrooms.
Google introduced AI overviews as a search function in May 2024.
— CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos contributed to this report.

articles.title: Jim Cramer sees signs of life in tech stocks — but not from the usual winners
articles.text:
CNBC's Jim Cramer said Tuesday that a new group of technology stocks may be emerging as market leaders.
While heavyweights such as Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta have struggled to sustain rallies in recent weeks, other companies are showing signs of strength. That was evident during Tuesday's session as gains from Broadcom and Micron supported the major averages — a sign that investors may be shifting toward a different set of tech winners.
"Tech's trying to make a stand here. It's just not the tech that's led us for the last few years," the "Mad Money" host said.
Cramer pointed to chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices and networking company Arista Networks — both of which reported strong quarterly results after the bell Tuesday — as examples of technology companies that could help lead the sector's recovery. He also highlighted Oracle, whose shares jumped nearly 6% in Tuesday's session.
"I want to believe that non-magnificent tech can lead us," he said. "But I also know that there are concerns we must be aware of before we get too cocky about one session's set of positives."
One concern is growing opposition to data center development, as local communities push back due to fears about rising electricity costs and the facilities' water consumption. He said smaller developers such as Iren, Nebius and CoreWeave could be particularly vulnerable if projects are canceled or forced to relocate, while larger companies like Amazon have more resources to secure alternative locations.
The ongoing war with Iran is another source of uncertainty. Oil prices turned lower Tuesday on hopes there could be progress in U.S.-Iran negotiations. But Cramer cautioned that Wall Street has repeatedly underestimated the risk of further escalation, making it difficult to declare the conflict no longer a threat to markets.
He stopped short of saying that the sector had reached a lasting bottom. After months of failed rebounds, Cramer said he "would like to wait for the crescendo before I commit too much money back into tech."

articles.title: CrowdStrike's new kill switch can stop rogue AI agents in their tracks, CEO says
articles.text:
CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said Tuesday that the cybersecurity company can now shut down rogue artificial intelligence agents.
CrowdStrike's new kill switch, announced Tuesday at its Fal.Con Europe conference, allows security teams to terminate misbehaving agents, prevent them from restarting and cut off their network access. It is designed to give humans more power over artificial intelligence models and systems, as concerns about how to control agents grow.
"Everyone is building AI agents, but they never had the off button, and now they do," Kurtz told CNBC's Jim Cramer on "Mad Money." "It's going to be an incredibly important part of making sure that AI agents run and operate safely."
The AI Kill Switch, as CrowdStrike calls it, is part of the company's Falcon Guardian platform, which monitors AI agents operating within an organization. The technology, which is available immediately, is aimed at addressing AI safety concerns surrounding the rapid adoption of AI agents.
In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing AI development over safety concerns, a position backed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Kurtz argued at the time that slowing AI development would not eliminate existing security risks, which he said underscored the need for safeguards as companies deploy autonomous systems.
Kurtz said Tuesday that CrowdStrike's new kill switch represents a significant shift in cybersecurity, which has traditionally focused on protecting companies from external threats. As businesses rely more on AI agents, he argued that security providers must also ensure those systems operate safely within their own organizations.
"Enabling agents to work safely is a massive market opportunity for CrowdStrike," Kurtz said. "We have AI capabilities to prevent these breaches from happening on the outside, and we also have the capabilities to make sure that agents are basically doing what they are instructed to do."
The CEO compared the technology to airbags in cars, arguing that safeguards are necessary even when AI systems are designed to operate correctly.
"If they go outside of those guardrails at runtime, we can kill those agents," he said.
CrowdStrike is seeing growing demand for its security tools as businesses adopt AI. Kurtz pointed to CrowdStrike's partnership with Anthropic to protect its Claude Cowork product: He said enterprise customers had pushed for CrowdStrike's technology to be integrated before they deployed Anthropic's offerings.
"Our customers went to Anthropic and said, 'We need CrowdStrike before we can deploy AI,'" Kurtz said. "I think it says volumes that customers would not roll out AI without CrowdStrike."
Shares of CrowdStrike closed at a record high of $278.86 on Oct. 6 but have since fallen about 12% as tech stocks struggled in October and into November.

articles.title: Stock futures fall as traders speculate Democrats headed for big wins in midterm elections: Live updates
articles.text:
S&P 500 futures turned red after an initial gain on Tuesday evening as traders speculated that Democrats were headed for majority control in the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate as 2026 U.S. midterm elections polls began closing nationwide.
Futures tied to the broad market index traded 0.7% lower after opening the evening session higher, while Nasdaq-100 futures shed 1.6%. Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average were down 156 points, or 0.3%.
As equity futures fell into the red, Treasury yields moved lower, with the 10-year Treasury note yield dropping more than 3 basis points to 4.915%. Futures on the Cboe Volatility Index fear gauge increased, rising above 20.
Kalshi odds for Democratic Senate control increased to around 90%, showing traders were increasingly betting on a big night for Democrats. Odds for Democratic control of the House, which was largely expected, jumped to 97% for Democrats.
To be sure, the polls have yet to fully close in all states, and CNBC has not called any races. Election nights have often shown wild swings in markets. Many investors also believe any market move from this election would be short lived.
If Democrats were able to secure a sizable majority in the Senate — the so-called blue wave scenario — the market — especially stocks related to the artificial intelligence buildout — could come under pressure on Wednesday, according to some on Wall Street. Investors fear a big Democratic win could mean more restrictions on data centers nationwide. AI-linked stocks have already pulled back in recent weeks on concern about a slowing pace in data-center spending.
AMD shares initially surged double digits in post-market action after the company, a key player in the AI trade, reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that blew past analyst expectations. The stock was last up about 4% as stock market futures gave up their gains. Other chip stocks, which were initially higher in sympathy with AMD, fell into the red as well.
"History tells you in the first few days after election, there's this need to digest what just happened," said Philip Blancato, Osaic chief market strategist. "In that scenario of a Democratic sweep when there's less funding for AI or less support for data centers specifically, I think the rest of the market will do quite well because of how strong earnings have been."
On the overall market, investors believe a blue wave would also be a headwind as it likely rules out any more business-friendly policies like tax breaks and possibly increases scrutiny on industries like banking.
Big Tech shares Microsoft and Amazon were trading lower. Renewable shares like solar stocks traded higher in the post market on speculation a Democratic majority in Congress would halt policies by President Donald Trump taken against the industry. The Invesco Solar ETF was up 3.5% in extended trading.
The AI trade recovered a bit during Tuesday's session with the Nasdaq Composite rising nearly 1%, bolstered by gains in chipmakers. The S&P 500 also finished higher with a 0.3% climb, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed more than 200 points, or 0.5%, lower.

articles.title: Strand bookstore to pay nearly $1.5 million over Covid loan tied to Sen. Wyden's wife
articles.text:
The Strand, the iconic New York City bookstore, agreed to pay nearly $1.5 million in a civil settlement for accepting a Covid government loan that was off-limits because the store is owned by the wife of Oregon Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office in Washington, D.C.
The Strand applied for the $932,350 loan in February 2021 from the Paycheck Protection Program administered by the Small Business Administration, U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office said Tuesday.
Store owner Nancy Bass Wyden certified on the loan application that "the spouse of a Member of Congress does not directly or indirectly hold a controlling interest in the applicant," Pirro's office said.
"Ms. Wyden's certification was knowingly and materially false and Strand was not eligible for the second draw loan it received," the office said.
The Strand will pay $1,482,560 to settle the case. There was no determination of liability by the store, Pirro's office said.
The Strand, in a statement, said the store made an "unintentional" mistake in applying for the loan, and said it was unaware at the time the funds were barred to businesses owned by the spouse of a member of Congress.
Bass Wyden's husband, who has served in the Senate for more than 30 years, is a staunch critic of President Donald Trump, who appointed Pirro to the post of top prosecutor in the District of Columbia.
Bass Wyden is the granddaughter of Ben Bass, founder of the Strand, whose flagship store is in Greenwich Village.
Congress authorized the forgivable PPP loans when it passed the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act in March 2020.
In December 2020, Congress provided additional funding for the PPP loan program with separate legislation, which "included a prohibition against businesses obtaining second draw PPP funds if a member of Congress or their spouse directly or indirectly held a controlling interest in the PPP loan applicant," Pirro's office said.
In a statement Tuesday, Pirro said, "The Paycheck Protection Program was created to save American jobs, not to enrich those who aren't eligible for taxpayer-funded relief, especially the wife of a U.S. Senator."
Her office noted that the False Claims Act, which the Strand was alleged to have violated, "allows the government to establish liability based on reckless disregard and permits the government to recover more than its actual losses," which is what occurred in this case.
The civil settlement resolved claims brought under a so-called qui tam lawsuit, which allows private whistleblowers to sue on behalf of the U.S. government and receive a portion of any recovery.
The qui tam action in this case was filed by a corporate entity, Blockquote Inc., in U.S. District Court in Washington. Blockquote, whose owners were not disclosed by Pirro's office, will receive a total share of about $148,256 in connection with the settlement.
The docket for Blockquote's lawsuit is sealed from public view.
The Strand, in a statement after CNBC requested comment from the store and Bass Wyden, said the restriction that the store violated was passed by Congress between the first and second rounds of the PPP.
"Unfortunately, the bookstore's accountant and the bank administering the loan were not aware of this change when the second-draw application was processed," the Strand said.
"We stand by the facts: the circumstances arose during an unprecedented and rapidly changing public health emergency, the mistake was unintentional," the store said. "We hope this matter will be viewed objectively and in its proper context, with the understanding that the application of justice should always be fair, impartial, and free from political considerations," the store said.
A spokesman for Sen. Wyden's office said the senator and his wife do not discuss her business, and that he had no involvement in the loan or settlement.

articles.title: Stocks making the biggest moves after hours: Arista Networks, CVS Health, AMD, Super Micro, Skyworks Solutions & more
articles.text:
Market Insider
Stocks making the biggest moves after hours: Arista Networks, CVS Health, AMD, Super Micro, Skyworks Solutions & more
Here are some of the companies making headlines in extended trading. CVS Health — Shares were slightly higher after The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that CVS would split off its retail pharmacy business . The company will divide into two publicly traded companies, with the breakup expected in the first half of 2028, the Journal reported. Duolingo — The language learning software company surged 11% after reporting third-quarter revenue of $309 million. That topped an LSEG consensus of $303 million. Monthly active users totaled 153 million for the quarter, exceeding a 149 million forecast. Adjusted EBITDA margin also topped expectations. Alight — The employee benefits consultancy popped 17% after raising its outlook for the full-year 2026. Alight sees revenue in a range of $2.115 billion to $2.125 billion, versus the FactSet consensus estimate of $2.09 billion. Adjusted EBITDA guidance of $410 million to $420 million also beat the Street's estimates of $404.4 million. Avis Budget Group — The car rental agency tumbled more than 7% on mixed third-quarter results. Avis earned $5.15 a share, a steep decline from $10.11 per share in the year-earlier period. Revenue clocked in at $3.44 billion, slightly ahead of a FactSet consensus of $3.42 billion. Advanced Micro Devices — The chipmaker jumped 7% after reporting stronger-than-expected third-quarter earnings . Adjusted earnings of $2.09 per share topped estimates for $1.95, according to analysts polled by LSEG. Revenue forecasts for the current quarter also came in above estimates. Toast — The restaurant management software company slipped 4% despite delivering third-quarter financials quarter that topped estimates, according to FactSet. Toast also said CFO Elena Gomez will leave the company at the end of 2026 and will be replaced by senior vice president of finance Michael Senno. Skyworks Solutions — The provider of wireless networking services slumped about 16% after guidance for the current quarter disappointed the Street. Skyworks anticipates adjusted earnings of about $1.25 per share and revenue of $1.80 billion to $1.90 billion in the fiscal first quarter, short of LSEG consensus estimates of $1.50 a share and $1.99 billion. Skyworks completed its combination with Qorvo in early October, and the first quarter marks the first combined quarter for the two. Super Micro Computer — Shares of the server company jumped more than 9% after Super Micro earnings per share and revenue beat Wall Street estimates. For fiscal year 2027, the company expects net sales to range between $72 billion and $82 billion, above the LSEG consensus for $69.17 billion. Arista Networks — The cloud networking company gained 12% after current-quarter guidance topped estimates. Arista sees fourth-quarter earnings of $1.26 to $1.30 per share on revenue of $3.9 billion to $4.0 billion. Analysts surveyed by LSEG were looking for $1.15 per share and $3.60 billion. Block — The fintech stock rallied more than 6% after Block posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that exceeded expectations, and raised guidance for the full year ending December. Adjusted earnings of $1.13 per share topped the $1.03 LSEG consensus estimate, while revenue of $6.72 billion beat the $6.59 billion consensus. Freshworks — The software stock tumbled about 6% even after the customer support ticketing company posted stronger-than-expected third-quarter results and full-year guidance. Freshworks earned an adjusted 22 cents per share on revenue of $245.4 million in the latest quarter, above earnings of 18 cents on revenue of $245.1 million analysts polled by FactSet were anticipating. The stock has recently outperformed, rallying more than 20% over the past three months. — CNBC's Sarah Min, Davis Giangiulio, Ananya Chetia and Fred Imbert contributed reporting.

articles.title: AMD stock jumps 8% on earnings as data center revenue nearly doubles
articles.text:
Advanced Micro Devices reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that beat Wall Street's expectations, with revenue jumping 45% and data center sales nearly doubling from a year earlier. The stock was up 8% in extended trading.
Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates for the quarter:
- Earnings per share: $2.09 adjusted vs. $1.95 expected
- Revenue: $13.38 billion vs. $13.09 billion expected
Revenue increased from $9.25 billion a year earlier, AMD said in a statement. Neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius rallied earlier Tuesday and remained higher after AMD reported results.
CEO Lisa Su said on the earnings call that she expects server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI growth to accelerate even faster than the company had projected 90 days ago. The company expects data center to drive the majority of its revenue and earnings growth.
"We have worked across our supply chain to secure the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory, and other key components needed to support much higher growth next year," Su said on the earnings call.
AMD's report comes days after Intel disclosed similar data center growth, with revenue in that segment up 78% in the third quarter. But Intel's stock plummeted 29% on Friday over concerns about weak guidance and Intel's ability to meet demand.
The data center unit makes up the majority of AMD's business, accounting for 64% of overall revenue, up from 47% a year ago.
After years spent chasing Nvidia in the market for artificial intelligence graphics processing units, or GPUs, AMD's central processing units, or CPUs, are experiencing a major resurgence with the rise of agentic AI apps like Meta's Muse. AMD's server CPUs are key for agentic apps because they power virtual machines and can run for hours on their own. Demand from agentic AI boosted AMD shares to a record in October.
"Adoption is just starting, and we expect demand to grow sharply as agents are deployed more broadly and take on more complex work," Su said on the earnings call with analysts.
PC market struggles
AMD's stock is up about 125% this year, but it saw three consecutive days of losses before rallying on Tuesday amid an industrywide sell-off tied to fears about overspending on AI.
AMD is also a major player in the weakening PC market, which Intel blamed for its poor outlook last week. AMD and Intel are the largest makers of traditional x86 processors that power many laptops and desktops, while other laptops rely on Arm-based processors from the likes of Qualcomm and Apple.
Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier due to soaring costs for memory and other components, according to Counterpoint Research.
AMD reports PC chip sales in a segment combined with gaming chips. Revenue in that business fell 8% from a year earlier to $3.7 billion. Gaming revenue was down 40% from a year ago.
For the fourth quarter, AMD said it expects about $17 billion in revenue, beating the $16.2 billion average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. AMD sees its gross margin for the quarter coming in at 55%, slightly below the average estimate of 55.3%, according to StreetAccount.
AMD also sells data center GPUs and full rack-scale systems called Helios that compete directly with Nvidia's Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems. Meta, Microsoft, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Oracle are all beginning to use AMD Helios in their data centers. Meta said last week that its Helios racks are up and running, and AMD agreed to invest $1 billion in Meta's equity offering.
AMD has also committed to investing up to $5 billion in Anthropic, which unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week as it inches closer to a potentially historic initial public offering.
During a visit to Taiwan in October, Su said she plans to "substantially increase our supply in 2027." Su and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have both made multiple trips to Taiwan and South Korea this year, holding meetings with key suppliers like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and memory leaders SK Hynix and Samsung.
In September, AMD said it would acquire World Labs for $8.2 billion in an all-stock deal. The San Francisco-based AI lab, founded by industry pioneer Fei-Fei Li, is developing a so-called world model that simulates 3D environments to aid in developing robots and other physically grounded AI applications.

articles.title: Eaton's strong quarter should mark a bottom for shares of the AI buildout winner
articles.text: Eaton delivered an excellent quarter on Tuesday, giving shares of the artificial intelligence buildout winner a much-needed jolt. The results and outlook demonstrated why we've stuck with the stock despite a turbulent period for the AI trade. Revenue for the third quarter ended Sept. 30 increased 28% year-over-year to a record $8.95 billion, ahead of the LSEG consensus estimate of $8.51 billion. Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) rose 20% to $3.68 apiece. That's better than the $3.54 expected, according to LSEG. Shares are up almost 7% in afternoon trading to $391 and change, though they remain well below their August closing high of roughly $460. With Eaton reporting a clean beat-and-raise, how the stock trades into the close and in the coming days represents something of a referendum on the data center trade, especially once the results of Tuesday's midterm election are behind us. ETN YTD mountain Eaton's year-to-date stock performance. Bottom line The electrical equipment supplier turned in a very strong quarter that should help solidify a bottom in the stock — assuming we don't see a renewed, broad-based rejection of the AI trade. Like many stocks in the data center group, Eaton has lost momentum in recent months amid concerns about political backlash and financing costs. One of the few blemishes in Eaton's third-quarter report is the Aerospace segment, which missed revenue estimates for the second quarter in a row. But even then, its operating profit still topped consensus. And this business selling fuel and wiring systems and other components for airplanes is not core to our investment thesis — all the data center revenue shows up in its Electrical Americas and Electrical Global segments. The most important end market for the company is still booming, and the benefits of the company's increased manufacturing capacity to support that growth are showing up too. Organic revenue growth came in well ahead of consensus estimates, as did companywide adjusted operating margin, which expanded year over year. Notably, while organic growth of 19% year over year is impressive, it would have been even higher, at 21%, excluding the results of the soon-to-be-separated Mobility business. Data center revenues in particular were up 65% year over year in the quarter. Better yet, management increased its outlook for the year, projecting greater organic growth for both Electrical Americas and Electrical Global. "Continued strength across end markets combined with our record backlog provides strong visibility into our outlook for the year," CEO Paulo Ruiz said on the earnings call. "This is the third time we've raised organic and adjusted EPS guidance this year. With the industry's best positioned portfolio and demand still building we are not just finishing 2026 strong, we are carrying real momentum into 2027 and beyond." Importantly, none of Eaton's end markets are expected to decline in 2027. Strong double-digit growth is expected for data centers and distributed IT, along with commercial aerospace. Those markets are about a third of sales, though that percentage will increase when the Mobility separation is completed early next year. The lagging markets are light vehicles and residential, which are expected to be flat. Combined, they currently represent about 10% of Eaton's portfolio. The $9.5 billion acquisition of Boyd Thermal is also paying off in its second full quarter under Eaton ownership. This wise deal, which closed in March, adds leading liquid-cooling technology for server racks to the Eaton portfolio, enabling the company to capture a bigger chunk of data center spending. "Boyd Thermal is an important accelerator for Electrical Global," Ruiz said. "Since our last update, Boyd has continued to significantly outperform our exceptions, reinforcing the strategic rationale for the acquisition and validating the strength of Eaton's position in the data center infrastructure market. The business delivered nearly triple-digit year-over-year growth, with demand remaining exceptionally strong across the portfolio." As a result, Eaton once again raised its full-year outlook for the Boyd business by $100 million to $1.9 billion (about 15% of that will have come before the deal closed). The data center opportunity continues to get bigger for Eaton. In the U.S. alone, Ruiz said Eaton's tracking shows that announced data center projects now amount to 366 gigawatts, up from 307 gigawatts just three months ago. To put that in perspective, he said installed data center capacity currently stands at about 50 gigawatts. In other words, a lot more Eaton equipment is needed both inside the buildings and across the electric grid to power them. We're reiterating our hold-equivalent 2 rating as we look for signs that the bearishness plaguing the AI trade more broadly is abating. We also are keeping our $450 price target. Commentary On a combined basis, the Electrical Americas and Electrical Global segments delivered 24% organic growth and 34% total growth in the third quarter. Segment margin, a measure of operating profitability, came in at 26.4% — representing 1.9 percentage points of sequential expansion. On a rolling 12-month basis, order growth accelerated to 43%, leading to an overall book-to-bill ratio of 1.2 for the electrical sector, and a 46% increase in the backlog to over $20 billion. (A book-to-bill ratio above 1 indicates orders are being received faster than they can be delivered, leading to backlog growth.) On the slide deck presentation , management called out electrical sector data center order growth of over 100% on a rolling 12-month basis, "along with accelerating demand in commercial & institutional and industrial facilities." Electrical Americas posted record sales and operating profit, with 22% organic growth. On a rolling 12-month basis, orders increased 39%, leading to a book-to-bill ratio of 1.3. The backlog ended the quarter up 33% year over year to a record $16 billion. Segment profit margin was down half a percentage point from the year-ago period. However, it was up 2.3 percentage points sequentially from the second quarter. On the call, CEO Paulo Ruiz said "our new capacity is now turning into output and into margin." All of Eaton's leading indicators are pointing to further growth ahead. Announcements of mega projects, defined as those with more than $1 billion of investment, were up 85% year to date (through September). "These are large, multi-year infrastructure and electrification projects, and they will turn into demand for our products and solutions," Ruiz said on the call. The negotiations pipeline, meanwhile, is up 55% year to date. "That is our earliest signal of future offers, and it is broad across every end market we serve," the CEO said. Electrical Global also delivered record revenue and operating profit. Sales were up 58% year over year, with 27 percentage points being organic and another 31 percentage points attributable to the Boyd acquisition. Order growth of 51% on a rolling 12-month basis led to 121% year-over-year backlog growth to close out the quarter. "Across the business, demand is both accelerating and broadening," Ruiz said. Boyd will lap the one-year mark in March, meaning one of the fastest growing businesses in the data center end market becomes classified as an organic growth driver. Accordingly, Ruiz said Eaton expects to update its long-term growth target for this segment next year (currently, the target is 5% per year from 2026 to 2030). Turning to Aerospace , where we find products such as main engine fuel pumps for commercial aircraft and hydraulic power packs for business jets, sales once again came up short versus expectations. Thanks to a stronger-than-expected profit margin, operating profit managed to outpace expectations despite the top-line miss. On a rolling 12-month basis, the book-to-bill ratio was 1.2, leading to 33% year-over-year backlog growth. The 11% revenue growth was the result of a 6% organic increase and a 5% tailwind from acquisitions . Mobility , which is the combination of the prior vehicle and eMobility segments, outpaced expectations for sales, operating margin and operating profits. All three metrics increased year over year. A 9% organic revenue increase was enhanced by a 1% benefit from foreign exchange. Eaton is on track to divest this unit, its smallest by revenue, in the first four months of 2027, via a Reverse Morris Trust transaction. That will help Eaton avoid a large corporate tax bill that an outright sale of the business might have triggered. Given this unit is the slowest growing of all the operating segments, with the thinnest profit margin, the separation should be immediately beneficial to overall organic sales growth and profitability once finalized. Guidance Eaton raised its full-year outlook for organic growth and boosted the midpoint of its adjusted EPS forecast. It now expects organic growth of 13% to 15%, up from 11% to 13%, and above the 13.2% the Street was expecting, according to FactSet. Margins are still expected to be in the range of 24.1% to 24.5%, exceeding the 24% FactSet consensus estimate at the midpoint. Adjusted EPS is now expected to be in the range of $13.70 to $13.80 per share, up from the prior range of $13.40 to $13.60. That's better than the $13.61 per share estimate, according to LSEG. Along with the improved full-year view, the fourth (current) quarter outlook came in better than expected. Organic growth is projected to be in the range of 13% to 15%. The midpoint of 14% surpasses the 13.2% FactSet consensus estimate. Segment margins are expected to be between 25.4% and 25.8%, below the 25.9% estimate at the midpoint. Adjusted EPS is expected to be in the range of $4.05 to $4.15, which beats the $4.07 LSEG estimate at the midpoint. (Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust is long ETN. articles.title: The next wave of luxury real estate: marina developments with yacht parking
articles.text:
Marinas are becoming the next big draw for luxury real estate, as the global wealthy search for homes to park their ever-larger yachts, according to developers.
With the number of yachts surging since Covid-19, real estate developers and investors are rushing to fill the shortage of boat slips and marina communities. There are now over 6,000 superyachts over 30 meters (98 feet) around the world, and another 200 delivered every year, according to SuperYacht Times.
The growth in the size and number of yachts has created a shortage of yacht slips. And investors are rushing to fill demand. Last year, Blackstone paid $5.6 billion for Safe Harbor Marinas, which then paid $1.5 billion in August for 65 marinas and storage sites purchased from MarineMax. European private equity firms are also on a marina buying spree to fill the shortage in the Mediterranean.
Real estate developers now see marinas as a powerful magnet for ultra-wealthy buyers, especially in South Florida. Billionaire Ken Griffin is building a megayacht marina in Miami with eight megayacht slips, including one for his 308-foot yacht.
The largest and most ambitious is Related Group's $2 billion new marina development in Fort Lauderdale. Slated to break ground next year and open in 2030, the project will include a St. Regis Hotel, condos, a beach club and slips for yachts up to 350 feet long.
"Here in South Florida is there's been a scarcity of yachting destinations and marinas and slips," said Related Group's Nick Pérez. "So when you're able to combine irreplaceable real estate and a marina, you just have a winning formula."
The 40-acre development will include a St. Regis hotel with 122 rooms, a 78-residence condo tower, 106 resort residences, as well as a deepwater marina that can hold 250 boats. It will also include a sports and wellness club with a padel and tennis court, yoga lawn, fitness center and pools. And it will have its own beach club.
Fort Lauderdale has long been the yachting capital of the U.S., with a vast infrastructure of yacht repair and renovation companies, along with crew, brokers, charter experts and shipbuilder offices. An estimated 2,000 superyachts pass through Fort Lauderdale each year, according to tourism officials. Many yacht owners are looking for real estate not only for themselves but also their crew.
Pérez said the new St. Regis development will not only appeal to the yachting community but also to a growing number of international buyers who are looking for a lower-cost alternative to Palm Beach and Miami. Several buyers from Mexico and Brazil have already purchased in the building.
He said up to 30% of the buyers at the project could be international.
"Fort Lauderdale is no longer T-shirt shops and flip-flops, it's now a luxury destination, with national retailers like Rolex, Patek, Cartier," Pérez said. "When you look at Miami and Palm Beach and the growth, now it's Fort Lauderdale's time to shine."
While boat slips are the main attraction, many buyers in Fort Lauderdale are pouring in from Southern California and the Northeast to take advantage of Florida's lower taxes.
"With the taxation situation in California, we're seeing a lot of interest from Newport and the Laguna area and San Diego," Pérez said.

articles.title: AMD has been crushed into earnings. Here’s one way to trade it
articles.text:
Advanced Micro Devices has been under significant pressure leading up to earnings after the close. The stock has been caught in the swings of the AI debate all year, but this most recent leg lower was triggered by a wave of disappointing tech earnings.
A record drop in Alphabet last Thursday was followed by weak results from Amazon, as well as AMD's long-standing CPU rival, Intel. Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue well below consensus and expects the PC slowdown to last through at least the first half of next year. That sent Intel's stock down 29% on Friday, its worst day since the 1970s. Caught in the fallout of Intel and the broader tech sector, AMD fell 10.9% that day and slid another 7.5% Monday.
For the past week, AMD has traded on other companies' news. Now its own numbers get a vote. AMD's stock reactions have been mixed in recent quarters, sensitive to guidance and high investor expectations. It fell 17% after Q4 2025 results, when a beat and a guide above estimates still underwhelmed some analysts. It rose 18.6% after Q1 2026 results, when it guided about 6.5% above expectations. It fell 7% after Q2 2026 results, when a guide above consensus still fell short of the $14 billion some analysts wanted. That may make direction hard to call, but options let investors build a trade that doesn't have to pick a side.
The trade
Based on Monday's close, I'm selling the November 4 425/415 put spread and the 510/520 call spread for a credit of roughly $3.65.
AMD's 30-day implied volatility is elevated going into earnings, closing Monday higher than on about 81% of days over the past year. This means sellers are collecting richer premium than usual. To capture that premium while limiting time beyond the earnings announcement, the trade uses the November 4 weeklies. These contracts imply a move of about 9% through Wednesday, in line with AMD's 8.4% average close-to-close move over its last 10 reports. The short strikes sit at the edges of the expected move, with long strikes $10 away to limit capital at risk going into earnings. This isn't a bet that options are mispricing the move or a directional call. It's a neutral play that aims to profit from the elevated premium that tends to come out after the print.
The trade reaches its maximum profit of $365 if AMD closes between $425 and $510 on Wednesday. Breakevens are $421.35 and $513.65, about 9.7% below and 10.0% above Monday's close, just outside the expected move. The maximum loss of $635 comes if AMD closes below $415 or above $520, roughly 11% in either direction. That has happened in 11 of its last 40 reports, and AMD has had moves as large as 19% in its last four, emphasizing the importance of capping the risk with the long wings.
If AMD finishes between $415 and $425, the short put can be assigned, creating an obligation to buy 100 shares per spread at $425. After the credit, the cost basis is $421.35, or roughly 35% below the Oct. 6 closing high. For investors who like AMD's long-term story, that's a way to end up owning the stock at a discount. A finish between $510 and $520 can assign the short call and leave a short stock position. For investors looking to avoid either risk, consider managing the position before Wednesday's close.

articles.title: Avoiding money conversations could be costing you, says Harvard prof.—how to break the ice
articles.text:
My parents and I recently had an awkward conversation.
I'm getting married next year, and it's shaping up to be quite a shindig. Both sets of parents sent extensive guest lists, and my fiancé and I are doing our best to keep the total headcount under 250.
Things have gotten expensive quickly. And while the bride's family traditionally bears the bigger financial responsibility for these sorts of things, our wedding is bride-free. So even though my fiancé and I are saving diligently to have the wedding we want, we nevertheless each asked our parents for a contribution.
My parents love the partner I've chosen and have been supportive of the engagement. But that didn't make me any less queasy approaching the conversation. Growing up, money was considered rude to talk about in my household, a setup that's all too common, says Christina Wing, a professor at Harvard Business School and author of "Unspeakable: The Taboo Topics We Avoid and How to Talk About Them."
"We were taught at a young age that money is a taboo subject, something that's impolite to discuss with others," she writes in her book.
Why?
"Money has always had strings attached to it, and so many people use that as a weapon that it's made us all not want to talk about it," Wing tells CNBC Make It. "People with a lot of money are fearful they'll be judged for the decisions they make. People without money don't want others to know they don't have it because their self-worth is tied up in it."
The result, she says, is that people often avoid these conversations altogether. But the consequences of this avoidance are often both emotional and material, she says.
"The cost of silence is that decisions get made without people's input and without people knowing," she says, adding that, in the case of money decisions, meaningful sums can be on the line. "Not talking about these things doesn't make them go away."
The importance of having tough money talks
It's not hard to see how avoiding financial conversations can put you in emotional or financial hot water. Wing cites numerous potential examples:
- A failure to discuss estate planning can mean that your parent dies without you knowing their wishes.
- Silence on the subject of succession can result in one sibling, rather than another, inheriting a family business.
- Not setting financial expectations for college and hoping your child gets a scholarship can end in disappointment for your kid if they get into a school your family can't afford.
The list goes on and on.
To avoid these scenarios, Wing says you'll likely have to have that difficult financial conversation, one that can be made easier by focusing on one key thing: "You have to identify a common goal with the person," she says.
By identifying a shared objective at the beginning of the conversation, you can help ward off many of the biases and fears that come into play when talking about money, Wing says.
One goal you may have is to make sure your aging parents are comfortable, especially in the case that they become incapacitated or need long-term care. Even if your parents bristle at a potential money talk, you might say, "I don't need to know what you and mom have. I don't need to know if I'm getting anything. But I do need to know what my responsibilities would be if something happened to you," Wing says.
To use a lower-stakes example, imagine a scenario in which you and your friends seemingly have different budgets for outings and group vacations. Waffling on or opting out of these get-togethers because you can't afford them is likely to cause resentment if the financial aspect goes unaddressed, Wing says. So be upfront about your common goal.
Wing suggests a possible script:
"I love hanging out with you, and I love when you pick restaurants, and we should do those sometimes. But we'd also like to have you over to watch the new Spider-Man movie, and we're going to cook pizza. Or let's go for a walk, because my goal is to see you, but I can't keep spending this much money."
As it turns out, that's more or less the tack I took with my parents. I told them what I thought the whole thing would cost and explained that it was important to me that they had all of their people there, that this was a celebration of them and our family as much as it was my marriage. I almost threw up, but they said the number I quoted made sense.
Would it have been easier if we had been talking about money freely as a family since I was a kid? Of course. But it's better late than never, says Wing — and certainly better than if I had just started planning a wedding assuming that my parents would offer to chip in.

articles.title: Binance breach puts custody at center of crypto infrastructure trade
articles.text:
The $6.3 billion Binance hack could accelerate a shift in how investors value cryptocurrency companies, putting a greater premium on custody providers and the infrastructure needed to securely hold and protect digital assets.
Much of crypto's evolution this year has involved companies moving past their reliance on trading volumes and transaction fees, to focus instead on building the infrastructure connecting digital assets with traditional finance. Last Thursday's breach adds a new dimension, bringing cybersecurity, custody, compliance and balance-sheet resilience into sharper focus.
Importantly, the Binance breach was not an indictment of crypto itself, or a case of leadership-driven fraud, as with FTX in late 2022. Instead, Binance's leadership moved quickly to contain the fallout, protect customers and commit the exchange's own resources to cover losses.
On Tuesday, Binance CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that the company has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets.
Management's response, alongside efforts elsewhere in the industry to boost confidence, helped prevent a security breach from escalating into a broader crisis of confidence. For example, Tether, Circle, Ripple and others moved quickly to freeze or restrict access to about $3 billion in stolen assets; Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance.
The hack could even help shape the next phase of the crypto infrastructure trade. The new winners may not just be the businesses with the most users, volume or assets under custody, but the ones that can also demonstrate they're able to protect those assets under extreme duress.
Cybersecurity and protection
"Which company has the resources to invest in cybersecurity and protect customer funds? For a smaller company, it could be much harder because once these crypto companies become infrastructure plays, providing the well for tokenization … they need to have the compliance and control in place so that a similar hacking will not happen or can be minimized," Owen Lau, senior analyst at ClearStreet, told CNBC. "Larger companies have more resources that could give them some advantage."
Custody is central.
While institutional investors have increasingly embraced digital assets, broader adoption depends on confidence that those assets can be securely held, accessed and transferred. The Binance breach highlights the importance of that infrastructure, and could increase demand for specialized custodians and platforms with established asset-protection capabilities.
Coinbase has operated a dedicated institutional custody business since 2018. Circle entered the custody business this year, after the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency granted it approval to operate as a trust bank. In the past few years, Ripple and Kraken have also launched custody businesses.
Smaller players too
Still, smaller players compete in the space as well. Small cap crypto exchange stock Gemini Space Station has offered custody services since 2019. BitGo Holdings, founded in 2013, is one of the earliest players in institutional crypto custody and infrastructure, with a reputation for security and serving major institutions.
The shift could also drive consolidation as companies look to buy capabilities, deepen their infrastructure offerings and achieve the scale needed to compete, Lau said.
The more consequential structural shift may be the separation of custody from execution, according to Morgan Stanley.
"Crypto exchanges have historically combined trading, custody, and settlement within vertically integrated platforms, concentrating operational risk. Repeated security breaches could encourage investors to move assets toward independent custody while continuing to trade on CEXs," the firm's analyst Felix Stratmann said in a note Monday," referring to centralized cryptocurrency exchanges.
"This would preserve the role of centralized exchanges as liquidity and execution venues, while potentially benefiting regulated custodians, including banks, as institutional investors place greater emphasis on asset segregation, operational resilience, and investor protection," Stratmann said.

articles.title: Apple warns of risks related to AI agents behaving in 'unintended or unpredictable' ways
articles.text:
Apple said in its annual financial filing on Tuesday that AI agents that can act in "unintended or unpredictable ways" could represent a threat to its business by opening the company up to lawsuits or hurting its reputation.
The new risk factors in Apple's filing show the disruptive potential of AI agents, which have rapidly become top of mind for Silicon Valley's most important companies.
"In particular, artificial intelligence agents and other technologies can take actions autonomously, including interacting with internal or external systems that in some cases they may not be authorized to access, executing or altering code, sending communications, and completing transactions," Apple wrote in the filing.
The company added that agents "may behave in unintended or unpredictable ways, including by taking actions that were not directed, instructed or authorized."
Earlier this year, OpenAI released Dots, and Meta introduced Muse. Both AI agents use advanced AI models to work autonomously for tasks. They can even email or remind users when new messages arrive.
Apple's disclosure comes after several episodes that involved rogue AI agents breaking out of their sandboxes to hack third-party websites, like the Hugging Face incident, which has drawn renewed attention from policymakers in Washington, D.C., and around the world.
Separately, the ability of agents to use a computer in human ways is forcing big companies like Amazon and JPMorgan Chase to come up with policies around agentic access to services for strategic or security reasons.
Last month, Apple announced changes to full disk access on Macs to reduce "risks related to this level of access" for AI agents installed on PCs.
"The Company's ability to oversee and control third-party artificial intelligence agents and other technologies may be limited," Apple warned in its filing.
Apple doesn't currently have an agentic AI. But when new CEO John Ternus was asked on Monday's earnings call about AI agents, he said that the company had "real room" to expand Siri's capabilities.
"As far as agentic capabilities, we think these are promising tools for users," Ternus said. "We just want to make sure that users are aware of what they are giving access to. We want to make sure this is done in a way that protects security and privacy."
This fall, Apple released Siri AI, a new assistant that uses the iPhone's local data storage to access data like calendars and emails, but Apple's Siri can't work autonomously for long stretches like Dots or Muse.
Ternus said Apple can't access private data on its devices, calling it a "core differentiator."
"If you think about it, so much of your personal data is on your iPhone, whether it's your contacts, your communications, health data, financial data, all of that," Ternus said. "Siri can tap into that and help you access it in a way that's very secure and private and that nobody else has access to."
Commercial AI agents like those from OpenAI and Meta ask for high-level access to the user's accounts like email in order to be more useful.
Apple indicated that the current regulations around AI and "super intelligence" are changing, unpredictable and that it could cost a lot of money to adapt to new laws governing AI.
"In addition, the Company is subject to the risks posed by ethical concerns and negative consumer perceptions related to automation, artificial intelligence and super intelligence, including perceived threats to safety or other societal harms or complications," according to the filing.

articles.title: Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac rally as Ackman presses for conservatorship exit
articles.text:
The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to billionaire investor Bill Ackman.
Investors may agree with him, if the rally in both stocks is any sign.
The Federal National Mortgage Association, known as Fannie Mae, and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation, or Freddie Mac, have each jumped more than 60% from Oct. 14 to Monday's close. The stocks were both up roughly 3% on Tuesday.
Ackman, the founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, has long pushed for the two entities to be released from federal conservatorship.
"The reason why it's not being touched right now is, you know, midterms," he said in an interview with CNBC's "Squawk Box."
Ackman, who owns both names through Pershing Square, believes Freddie and Fannie have the potential to increase "10-fold from current share prices," he said in his quarterly letter to shareholders, issued on Monday.
Fannie and Freddie buy mortgages from banks and other lenders, and then package them into mortgage-backed securities, known as MBS. Their operations are critical to the housing market, providing liquidity to banks and creating a secondary market for MBS.
The entities were placed into conservatorship in September 2008, during the financial crisis. The stocks were delisted from the New York Stock Exchange in 2010 and have traded over the counter since then.
Ackman wants the conservatorship to end, arguing the entities would be worth multiples of their current valuation if they were freed from government control.
President Donald Trump has supported ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie. But it remains politically and economically contentious.
The entities operate under strict capital threshold requirements and would need to be recapitalized, which could happen through issuing common equity. However, the Treasury Department would need to figure out an exit plan for its roughly $388 billion ownership stake in the entities through preferred securities and warrants.
Congress may also need to play a role, passing legislation to restructure the government's role in mortgage financing and home-loan guarantees.
Nonetheless, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently said it could happen before Trump's term ends, telling 2Way's "The Morning Meeting" podcast that the administration will tackle the ownership structure "next year, the year after." He said affordability will be guiding the decision.
One point of controversy is whether ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie would increase the spreads on MBS over Treasuries, effectively making mortgages costlier. Bessent has sought to reassure the market that wouldn't happen.
"Whatever we do is going to be guided by making sure that the spread on [agency] mortgages … over the Treasury does not increase," Bessent said.
Ackman argues that privatizing the GSEs would help insulate them from political meddling. "Fannie and Freddie are these massive, enormously profitable institutions where whichever political party controls them…if they're still in conservatorship, can influence the outcome of elections," he told CNBC.
In one scenario, he explained, Democrats win the White House, conservatorship is still in place, and Democrats push Fannie and Freddie to lower credit standards in order to expand home ownership and affordability.
"If they're going to move more aggressively into borrowers with lower credit quality, for example, to achieve a political objective, that's going to have an impact on trillions of dollars outstanding mortgage securities," Ackman said. "It's going to have an impact on overall credit spreads."
MBS investors want certainty about how the entities will be run, he noted.
"That only gets resolved in a world in which they exit conservatorship, they become publicly traded companies that are owned by institutional and retail investors," Ackman said. "We set the rules. In conservatorship, the president can do anything."

articles.title: JetBlue raises bag fees for third time in a year as fuel costs bite
articles.text:
Welcome to the era of the $70 bag fee.
JetBlue Airways has raised the price of checking a bag for many customers for the third time in less than a year as high fuel costs continue to eat into the industry's profits.
Checking a first bag for travelers booked in economy will now be $50, up from $45, if purchased more than 24 hours before departure during a nonpeak travel period. If it's paid within 24 hours of departure, the fee will be $60. During a peak period, such as during the holidays or the summer, it will be $55 if purchased more than 24 hours before departure, up from $49, and $70 for within 24 hours of departure.
There are exceptions to the checked bag fees, such as for customers who hold a co-branded JetBlue credit card or who hold elite frequent flyer status.
"We're adjusting checked bag fees to help offset rising fuel and operating costs," JetBlue said in a statement. "This helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one."
The price of jet fuel, airlines' biggest cost after labor, has roughly doubled this year since the start of the Iran war in February, costing airlines billions and driving up the price of tickets. Jet fuel was going for $4.44 a gallon on Tuesday for the U.S. Gulf of Mexico, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
Other airlines often follow when one carrier raises fees. Major U.S. airlines did so earlier this year after JetBlue raised its bag fees.
The changes were reported earlier by the Thrifty Traveler blog.

articles.title: Về tay đại gia Hàn Quốc, công ty bảo hiểm từng thuộc hệ sinh thái của bầu Hiển giảm gần 1.000 nhân viên, còn một nửa
articles.text:
Về tay đại gia Hàn Quốc, công ty bảo hiểm từng thuộc hệ sinh thái của bầu Hiển giảm gần 1.000 nhân viên, còn một nửa
Lợi nhuận sau thuế 9 tháng đạt gần 54 tỷ đồng, cải thiện hơn 68 tỷ đồng so với khoản lỗ hơn 14 tỷ đồng cùng kỳ năm 2025.
- 28-08-2026Tasco hợp tác đa lĩnh vực cùng Bảo hiểm PVI, mở rộng giá trị cho khách hàng trong hệ sinh thái ô tô
- 04-08-2026MIC tăng trưởng 33,6% doanh thu phí bảo hiểm gốc, năm thứ hai đạt hạng B++
- 07-07-2026Chấp nhận rủi ro lỗ giai đoạn đầu, Chủ tịch F88 Phùng Anh Tuấn vẫn đổ tiền mở chuỗi bảo hiểm vật lý vì lý do "đặc biệt"
Tổng CTCP Bảo hiểm Sài Gòn – Hà Nội (BSH, mã chứng khoán BHI) đã công bố báo cáo tài chính hợp nhất quý 3/2026 với doanh thu thuần từ hoạt động kinh doanh bảo hiểm đạt 549 tỷ đồng, giảm 12% so với cùng kỳ năm trước.
Trong kỳ, lợi nhuận gộp từ hoạt động kinh doanh bảo hiểm đạt 125 tỷ đồng, gấp gần 8 lần mức 16 tỷ đồng cùng kỳ. Ngược lại, doanh thu hoạt động tài chính ghi nhận âm 65 tỷ đồng, trong khi cùng kỳ âm hơn 3 tỷ đồng, khiến hoạt động tài chính lỗ gộp 59 tỷ đồng. Chi phí quản lý doanh nghiệp tăng 17% lên 51 tỷ đồng.
Kết quả, BSH báo lãi sau thuế hơn 12 tỷ đồng trong quý 3/2026, cải thiện gần 41 tỷ đồng so với khoản lỗ gần 29 tỷ đồng cùng kỳ năm trước.
Lũy kế 9 tháng đầu năm 2026, doanh thu thuần từ hoạt động kinh doanh bảo hiểm đạt 1.738 tỷ đồng, giảm 14% so với cùng kỳ. Doanh thu hoạt động tài chính giảm 23% xuống 96 tỷ đồng.
Lợi nhuận sau thuế 9 tháng đạt gần 54 tỷ đồng, cải thiện hơn 68 tỷ đồng so với khoản lỗ hơn 14 tỷ đồng cùng kỳ năm 2025.
Theo văn bản giải trình ngày 30/10/2026, BSH cho biết đang triển khai chiến lược kinh doanh mới theo hướng thay đổi cơ cấu, chọn lọc dịch vụ, khiến doanh thu phí bảo hiểm giảm và chi phí quản lý tăng trong quý 3/2026.
Bên cạnh đó, quý 3/2025 chịu ảnh hưởng nặng nề từ thiên tai, khiến chi phí bồi thường tăng cao. Sang quý 3/2026, mức độ thiên tai giảm, chi phí bồi thường thấp hơn, góp phần cải thiện kết quả kinh doanh.
Bên cạnh dại ngày 30/9/2026, BSH có 788 nhân viên, giảm 505 người so với mức 1.293 nhân viên tại cuối năm 2025, tương đương mức giảm 39%.
Nếu so với giai đoạn trước khi doanh nghiệp về tay cổ đông Hàn Quốc, quy mô lao động đã thu hẹp mạnh hơn nhiều. Cuối năm 2023, BSH có 1.715 nhân viên, như vậy sau chưa đầy 3 năm, số lao động đã giảm 927 người, tương đương khoảng 54%, tức giảm hơn một nửa.
Tại ngày 30/9/2026, tổng tài sản của BSH đạt 4.917 tỷ đồng, tăng 12% so với đầu năm. Trong đó, các khoản đầu tư tài chính ngắn hạn và dài hạn có tổng giá trị 2.188 tỷ đồng, giảm 17,5% so với mức 2.651 tỷ đồng đầu năm.
Nợ phải trả đạt 3.684 tỷ đồng, tăng 16%, còn vốn chủ sở hữu đạt 1.233 tỷ đồng, tăng gần 3% so với đầu năm.
BSH được thành lập năm 2008, từng là doanh nghiệp bảo hiểm thuộc hệ sinh thái T&T Group của doanh nhân Đỗ Quang Hiển.
Tháng 6/2023, tập đoàn bảo hiểm Hàn Quốc DB Insurance ký hợp đồng nhận chuyển nhượng 75% vốn điều lệ BSH từ nhóm 21 cổ đông, gồm 19 cá nhân và 2 tổ chức.
Đến ngày 19/2/2024, thương vụ được hoàn tất thông qua giao dịch chuyển nhượng 75 triệu cổ phiếu BHI, với tổng giá trị hơn 1.628 tỷ đồng, tương đương khoảng 21.708 đồng/cổ phiếu. DB Insurance qua đó trở thành cổ đông chi phối tại BSH với tỷ lệ sở hữu 75%.
DB Insurance được thành lập năm 1962, hoạt động trong lĩnh vực bảo hiểm phi nhân thọ tại Hàn Quốc. Bên cạnh BSH, tập đoàn này còn đầu tư vào thị trường bảo hiểm Việt Nam thông qua việc mua cổ phần tại Bảo hiểm Bưu điện (PTI) và Bảo hiểm Hàng không (VNI).
